56467e994c0b9a0f: LONDON: UK author M. John Harrison won the Booker Prize on Monday for his enigmatic novel "The End of Everything", which echoes concerns about artificial intelligence in a darkly satirical depiction of post-apocalyptic Britain.
Harrison, 81, became the oldest winner of the award, which comes with a £50,000 (US$67,000) prize and a boost in sales and profile for the winner.
A veteran of the British science fiction literary scene, it was Harrison's first time being shortlisted for the coveted prize, which critics have said was long overdue.

He beat shortlisted authors Marlon James, Douglas Stuart, Elizabeth Strout, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry, whose entries ranged from a queer epic unfolding in 1980s Kingston to a campus satire set in modern-day London.
"The End of Everything" came out "ahead in terms of both its extraordinary expert writing, but also huge ambition," chair of the judges Mary Beard told a press conference.

Harrison's 13th novel follows the beachcomber Phillip Tennent and his dementia-stricken, free-spirited aunt Marnie, set in the near-future on the windswept English coast invaded by mysterious objects known as the iGhetti.

An unnamed catastrophe plunges the characters into a murky post-apocalyptic world where the European continent seems to have disappeared and the arrival of the iGhetti, which can imitate humans, evoke interactions with artificial intelligence.
"One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible," Beard said, adding the book spoke to the present "moment."
"This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future," Beard said in a statement.
In dream-like episodes this tight, 198-page novel alludes to Brexit, the Covid-19 pandemic and the invasion of technology into daily life.

As is often the case with Harrison's writing, which has been described as genre-bending and singular, the plot counts less than the atmosphere, and the author's elliptical and poetic style heightens the feeling of gradual collapse.
- AI CONCERNS -

"Current affairs provided the themes and the satire," Harrison said of his book. "What happens when all of our expectations and explanations of the world become an ongoing disaster, but we still have to make a life?"
The author previously said he was inspired by the 2008 financial crisis, and wanted to write a novel about the "failure of explanation in society."

Born in Rugby, England, in 1945, Harrison, is the author of numerous science fiction books, including the Viriconium saga (1971-1984) and "Light" (2002), the first volume of a trilogy known as The Kefahuchi Tract, renowned as major works of the genre.
Little known to the general public beyond circles of science fiction enthusiasts, when he was shortlisted, The Telegraph newspaper wrote: "Finally, he's getting his due."
The theme of artificial intelligence has been on the judges' minds through the year-long selection process, which saw them whittle down 163 entries to a shortlist of six novels.
Beard pointed out concerns surrounding AI were "pretty high on this book."
"Phillip has got this object, this artefact, and it's not clear how sentient it is. It's not clear what it is," Beard said in a press conference to announce the winner.
In an earlier interview with AFP, Beard said the prize-awarding panel would have to think about the role of AI in publishing and writing in the coming years.
"I think for the future it's inevitable that that will be on the agenda. You can't bury your head in the sand about that," she said.
The other judges have talked about wanting to create a shortlist of books that were distinctly human, and could not be replicated by AI.
The prize, which celebrates the best work of long-form fiction by writers of any nationality, written in English and published in the last year, was awarded on Monday at a London ceremony.
Last year, British-Hungarian author David Szalay won the prize for "Flesh", his tortured tale of a Hungarian emigre in London.--AFP

4e7ce7c1eec68ea5: LONDON: Once homeless and destitute, Brighton have defied the odds to emerge as the most unexpected Premier League title contenders since Leicester's fairytale run a decade ago.
Brighton head into the international break proudly sitting second in the Premier League after Sunday's 2-0 win against Brentford.
Fabian Hurzeler's side have moved above far wealthier clubs including Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea, with leaders Arsenal only five points ahead of the high-flying Seagulls.
Brighton's climb towards the top of the table could easily be written off as a brief blip before the league's traditional powers reassert their supremacy.

But that would be to ignore the rock-solid foundations laid by Hurzeler and Albion's astute owner Tony Bloom, a professional gambler who has transformed Brighton since taking a major gamble when he bought the club in 2009.
Brighton have won seven of their 10 league games this season, a blistering run that included a pair of statement victories.
Swatting aside champions Arsenal 3-0 in September while wearing a commemorative kit to mark the club's 125th anniversary was a memorable afternoon.

But beating City 1-0 in Manchester in October – just days after losing a League Cup penalty shoot-out at the Etihad Stadium – showed Brighton have the bloody-minded streak required to cope with the pitfalls of a title race.

In a season in which City are distracted by their appeal against a guilty verdict for financial breaches, Liverpool and Chelsea are rebuilding under new managers and Manchester United are in disarray, there could be an opening for Brighton to replicate Leicester's fairytale title triumph in 2016.
Catching Arsenal will not be easy but Hurzeler admitted there is mounting excitement around his club.
Asked when supporters could start to dream of a title bid, Hurzeler said: "They should be always excited if they watch our game, and that's our job to make them excited.
"I always say they can dream, they can have high expectations on us, but these are things we can't control."
Hurzeler became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when Bloom lured him from St Pauli in 2024.
Born in Texas, the 33-year-old German had a modest playing career before turning to coaching, where he caught Bloom's eye by leading St Pauli into the Bundesliga.
His work at Brighton has been even more impressive, taking them to a pair of eighth place finishes in the Premier League and into this season's UEFA Conference League.
- STAMPEDING BULL -
Bloom has also been a gleeful disruptor of football's establishment.
When lifelong fan Bloom purchased Brighton, they were languishing in the third tier with significant debts and playing at a ramshackle athletics stadium on the outskirts of the town.
Implementing the ground-breaking use of analytics and advanced scouting technology, Bloom has helped Brighton sign unknown youngsters and turn them into top-level stars.
He brought Brighton back to a purpose-built new stadium in 2011, sparking a golden era that serves as a stark contrast to their chaotic past.
"Anyone walking into Brighton today compared to even 15 years ago would not think it was the same football club," sporting director Mike Cave said.
In keeping with the hipster seaside town's colourful community, Brighton has always been one of English football's more eccentric outposts since their foundation in 1901.
Trophies might have been in short supply on the South coast, but Brighton have a habit of giving their fans unforgettable moments – for better or worse.
A 1983 FA Cup final appearance against Manchester United featured a famous miss by Gordon Smith that could have secured the club's first major silverware.
Brighton were thrashed by United in the replay and crashed out of the top-flight the same season.

An even more catastrophic relegation from the Football League in 1997 was only avoided on the last day of the season after a live bull – used as Hereford's mascot – stampeded onto the pitch during a dramatic draw that saved Brighton from potential oblivion.
The club spent two years in exile, playing their matches 70 miles from Brighton at Gillingham, after the Goldstone Ground, their home since 1902, was sold because of escalating debts.
From the depths of despair, Brighton have emerged unscathed.
"What got this football club through was the determination of its fans. The bucket collections. The protests. The refusal to accept the Albion should disappear," Bloom said.
Whether their dreams of Premier League glory are fulfilled or not, the mere possibility is already a footballing miracle.--AFP

MOSCOW: Approximately 20,000 convicted foreign nationals remain in the United Kingdom following their release from custody despite active deportation orders against them, Sputnik/RIA Novosti reported, citing The Times newspaper and official data from the UK Home Office.
According to the newspaper, the proportion of deported criminals remains critically low, even though the number of individuals removed from the country has risen from 8,000 in 2020 to 36,000 in 2025.
Foreign criminals still account for less than 30 per cent of the total number of people removed from the UK, the publication said.

Up to June 2025, 20,000 foreign offenders were living freely in the community despite being subject to deportation orders. For some countries, the return rates are so low that fewer than one in 20 can expect to actually be deported, the publication noted.

The Times pointed out that the deportation rate for criminals to Nigeria and Jamaica has fallen below five per cent, while for Somalia, Sierra Leone and the Congo, it ranges from 0.6 per cent to 2.7 per cent.
Migrants often seek to reach the UK illegally and obtain refugee status.

In 2025, more than 41,000 migrants arrived in Britain illegally by boat across the English Channel — the second-highest figure on record, following the peak seen in 2022. At that time, more than 45,700 migrants reached British shores.
The UK authorities are spending several million pounds a day on accommodating asylum seekers in hotels. — BERNAMA
15226a4d302dd853: LONDON: Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker has urged the club to extend his successful stay at Anfield by handing him a contract beyond this season.
Becker has played a key role in Liverpool's Premier League and Champions League triumphs since signing from Roma in 2018.
The 34-year-old Brazilian has made 347 appearances for the Reds, winning seven major trophies.
Becker is out of contract at end of the current campaign and has been linked with a move, but is keen to prolong his time on Merseyside with a new deal.
"Yes (I want to stay), in my mind. I'm focused on playing every game but in my mind I'm happy to stay," Alisson said after Sunday's 3-1 win at Crystal Palace in the Premier League.
"That depends on a lot of aspects and different situations. But my will is to stay. I'm happy here and my family is happy here.
"I'm still hungry for titles and to (keep) delivering good performances. I still want to play at the top level for as long as I can, so that's my thinking."
Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola recently said he hoped the 'keeper could "continue for more time" with his team.
Becker revealed "my agent is talking with the club" after a close-season that featured talk of a potential switch to Juventus.
He underlined his enduring value with a fine performance to help Liverpool beat Palace.
But Giorgi Mamardashvili is waiting in the wings as Becker's solid deputy, with teenage 'keeper Lucca Brughmans set to join Liverpool from Genk next year.
"Our reality is that we're not doing as well as we can. The consistency is not there yet," Becker said of Liverpool's inconsistent start to the season.

"We have a top manager, top players. We are capable of great things but as a team we need to get to a point where we feel: 'We are OK now. We have the confidence. We have everything that's needed to win.'"--AFP
bf90291d6cdbd6af: WASHINGTON: A Republican lawmaker moved Monday to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran, setting up a potentially explosive vote in Congress days after President Donald Trump's party suffered a crushing midterm defeat.
Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorisation and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
The Republican-controlled House could vote as early as Wednesday, with some lawmakers from Trump's party signaling they might join Democrats in backing the charges.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio came to Hegseth's defence Monday while visiting Paris.
"I think it's unfair. Look, I think Pete's done a good job, I really do," Rubio told reporters, praising his colleague as hardworking and "incredibly smart."
Rubio credited Hegseth with helping build counter-cartel partnerships in the Americas, severely weakening Iran's military and overseeing the operation to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.

Impeachment would be a humiliating blow for the Trump administration, but would not automatically remove Hegseth. Conviction requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate – a much higher hurdle, even after Democrats take control in January.
The move has gathered momentum since Tuesday's midterms, when Democrats swept both chambers amid voter anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices.
Republicans retain control until the new Congress takes office on Jan 3, but their defeat has fuelled recriminations. Defeated Republicans could skip votes, making impeachment easier to pass.
- 'HARD YES' -
Massie, a Trump critic who lost his primary to a candidate backed by the president, is using a special procedure requiring the House to consider his resolution within two legislative days.
Hegseth had "knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders" by waging war without congressional approval, Massie said on the House floor.
His articles allege violations of the 1973 War Powers Resolution, as well as misconduct involving civilian casualties and operations in Yemen and Venezuela.
The Pentagon has rejected the allegations.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become speaker in January, said Sunday he was a "hard yes" on impeachment.
"The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," Jeffries told ABC News.
"Pete Hegseth has got to go."
- UNLIKELY REMOVAL -
Some Republicans are wavering. Arkansas congressman French Hill said he wanted to hear the debate before deciding whether the accusations merited impeachment.
Under the Constitution, the House can bring impeachment charges by a simple majority. The Senate then holds a trial, with two-thirds of senators present needed to convict and remove the official.
Democrats would need substantial Republican support even after they take the Senate majority. Only two Cabinet secretaries have been impeached in US history, and neither was removed by the Senate.

Hegseth has called Massie's effort a "sham" and dismissed him as a "disgruntled" congressman. The Pentagon has scheduled a rare Hegseth press briefing Tuesday, while Trump has publicly vowed to keep him in office.

Republican congressman Don Bacon questioned Massie's reasoning but argued Hegseth deserved impeachment for withholding aid to Ukraine and forcing out or blocking promotions for around 80 senior military officers.
"There's a bunch of us have been talking about it," Bacon told CNN, urging Hegseth to resign.--AFP

BUDDING actor Muhammad Amir Haiqal Azhar may be unfamiliar to many Malaysians, but the 27-year-old from Semenyih, Selangor, has sparked pride among K-drama fans here with his Malay lines in two South Korean series.
He thrilled viewers with "Woi, nak pergi mana woi" in 'Taxi Driver 3' and recently went viral in 'Dead-End Job' saying "berhenti semua, berhenti" and "hati-hati dengan ketua kau".
Speaking to Bernama, Amir Haiqal said he entered the industry by chance while studying production at Konkuk University in Seoul, after a friend persuaded him to join an acting class.
"It was through that class that I overcame my fear of performing in front of a crowd and discovered my passion for acting.
"I am proud to represent Malaysia in Korean dramas, especially through Malay dialogue. But this is just the beginning of my acting journey in South Korea."
Breaking into the scene requires two to three rounds of auditions — from profile and video submissions to in-person castings. He also helps craft his Malay lines.
"The scripts are usually given in Korean and I am asked to translate them into Malay. Some lines are added spontaneously during filming."
He has appeared in seven dramas, two feature films, eight indie films, two theatre productions and three YouTube dramas, learning from seasoned actors like Ko Chang-seok and Lee Min.
Having completed his studies, he plans to stay in South Korea rather than return immediately.

"I intend to keep chasing acting opportunities here, become one of the actors directors actively seek out and eventually land leading roles in both Korean dramas and films," he said, adding that he remains open to Malaysian projects.
ef2cbfafae97d2e7: NEW YORK: US stocks rallied on Monday, as a drop in oil prices tempered inflation fears and helped the S&P 500 rebound from its biggest weekly drop since April 2025, and tech shares jumped even as AI heavyweight Nvidia slumped with controversy swirling around CEO Jensen Huang.
Last week, stocks slumped after a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.

Each of the 11 major S&P 500 sector indexes rose on the session, with nine showing gains of more than 1% on Monday. Industrials and consumer discretionary were the top performers, rising more than 3% each.
Nvidia falls

Markets were in rally mode even as Nvidia, the second-most valuable company in the world, tumbled 4.2% and closed at its lowest level since April 7. Investors questioned CEO Huang's future at the AI chipmaker after an internal investigation into whether a foreign intelligence effort had targeted him.

"The AI story is not going away if people are worried about that, the Democrats are not going to destroy AI. They can't. It's got a life of its own. They can put regulation around it, but they're certainly not stopping it," said Ken Polcari, partner and chief market strategist at SlateStone Wealth in Jupiter, Florida.
Providing further support was a sharp drop in crude oil prices that helped dampen concerns about price pressures, as US president Donald Trump downplayed the likelihood of renewed strikes on Iran.
"Oil prices for sure, if they're down, that's certainly adding fuel to the fire," said Polcari.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,104.02 points, or 2.15%, to 52,389.75, the S&P 500 gained 173.08 points, or 2.35%, to 7,549.94 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 673.71 points, or 2.74%, to 25,253.14.
The S&P recorded its biggest daily percentage gain since April 8, while the Nasdaq marked its biggest daily advance since July 30.
Inflation readings are on the docket this week as the labour department will release its Consumer Price Index report for October on Tuesday and Producer Price Index on Friday.
Analysts see overreaction

Some analysts on Wall Street also viewed last week's decline as an overreaction. Morgan Stanley and UBS said last week's rout in AI stocks was overdone, and risks were low of extreme regulation of data center developments, even with Democratic majorities in the US Congress.

Even as oil prices have eased, expectations for a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December policy meeting remain above 80%, according to CME FedWatch, as October's strong jobs report gave the central bank latitude to continue raising rates.
On Monday, Richmond Federal Reserve president Tom Barkin said the Fed should move its monetary policy "with care" as it maps a response to inflation.

Chipmakers surged. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index shot up 6.9% after plunging more than 12% last week, its biggest weekly drop since the week ended April 4, 2025. Nvidia was the sole decliner in the index on Monday, while Broadcom, up 8.8%, and Advanced Micro Devices, up 13.3%, were the two biggest boosts.

Shares of investment giant KKR advanced 1.7% after its quarterly profit hit a record high. Constellation Energy, an energy firm with exposure to the AI buildout, shot up more than 10% after its adjusted third-quarter profit surpassed expectations.
Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 4.06-to-1 ratio on the NYSE, and by a 3.34-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq.
The S&P 500 posted 16 new 52-week highs and three new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 103 new highs and 164 new lows.
Volume on US exchanges was 18.98 billion shares, compared with the 18.72 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

SUNDERLAND: Sunderland hauled themselves off the bottom of the Premier League as Enzo Le Fee's penalty earned a huge 1-0 win over Chelsea for embattled boss Regis Le Bris.
The Frenchman was under pressure after a dismal 2-0 home defeat to Dinamo Zagreb in the Europa League on Thursday put his position in doubt ahead of an international break.
Sunderland, though, bounced back for a huge three points thanks to two controversial penalty decisions.
Chelsea were furious that Cole Palmer was not awarded a spot-kick for a foul by Luke O'Nien moments before the only goal of the game.
A VAR review deemed the contact made was outside the area and therefore could not be overturned.
Sunderland were awarded a penalty at the other end 10 minutes before half-time.
The visitors were again aggrieved that Levi Colwill was adjudged to have fouled Brian Brobbey as both players grappled in their attempt to reach the ball.
Le Fee dispatched the resulting spot-kick past Mike Penders and Sunderland held on for just a second league win of the season.
Speaking about both incidents, Alonso said: "I haven't seen Cole's one, but I've been told that there was a chance that it would be a fair penalty and it could have been given.
"The other one, not happy with how we defended that situation, something that we could avoid. From that action to give a penalty is not good from us."
Chelsea missed the presence of Joao Pedro up front as Palmer and Morgan Rogers were kept in check by the home side.
A fourth defeat in 10 league games under Xabi Alonso leaves the Blues in fifth, two points outside the top four.
"I think we didn't deserve more than probably one point, the game was really close," Alonso said.
"We were against the low block, we missed a bit of patience, a bit of quality, creativity in the last third to create more chances.
"We need to be more consistent to move the ball from one side to the other, we didn't do good enough." — AFP
40a7e439b1c9008b: It's barely been two months since the controversial Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and we've already got a shockingly unexpected ouster: Co-CEOs of the rebooted DC Universe, James Gunn and Peter Safran, are stepping down from that role despite the Hollywood rumor mill assuming that the duo would be safe.

We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow.

DCU fans are mourning the news and what it could mean for the franchise. My feelings are mixed. Gorilla Grodd—described as a “mockumentary crime comedy superhero series.”
aea1356f4a58858f: PARIS: European foreign ministers on Monday pressed US secretary of state Marco Rubio at a G7 meeting in Paris to ensure any settlement in the war with Russia is fair to Ukraine, ahead of US-mediated talks on ending the conflict.

European capitals have insisted that they must be represented at the table in the negotiations in Abu Dhabi and some have also expressed wariness about intensifying American talk of a new security architecture for Europe.

The meeting of ministers from the leading industrialised nations of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US provides Europe and its allies with a chance to air concerns with their US counterpart.

Russia's war against Ukraine following the February 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbour is grinding towards its fifth anniversary. And Washington is still not ruling out new attacks against Iran even after the defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans in last week's midterm elections.
The meeting coincides with US-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi, scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday, on ending the Ukraine war.

"It is certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change" to Europe's existing security architecture, said German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul after talks with Rubio.
"Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe -- only with Europe," he added.
French foreign minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Sunday that Europeans would be represented at the Abu Dhabi talks, with France also participating.
Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a "very big" deal with Russia involving not only Ukraine but "all of Europe".

But before leaving for Paris, Rubio said the post-war security infrastructure of Europe is "one of the key topics that's been raised repeatedly in every conversation any time negotiations have been discussed".
"We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point," he noted.
Europe security concerns
President Trump's son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner meanwhile said Russia and Europe must hold direct talks on "broader security arrangements" as part of any Ukraine peace deal.
"We recognise the difficult decisions ahead," he said.
Speaking in Bucharest, EU commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said Russia must halt fighting in Ukraine before "meaningful" talks can be held on broader security arrangements in Europe.
Ukraine's foreign minister Andriy Sybiga will be joining the talks in Paris for a session on Ukraine on Tuesday.
Before leaving for Paris, he said: "No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs."

Wadephul said the Abu Dhabi talks must show whether Russia is "genuinely prepared to negotiate", urging Moscow to "give up maximalist demands" and warning against any "negotiation show" in the UAE capital.

He warned that against a background of continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure "we see no substantial contribution whatsoever toward negotiations gaining any serious momentum" on Moscow's part.

But in an interview with AFP, Canada's foreign minister Anita Anand hailed the "importance" of US-mediated talks, saying it was "positive" that both sides were willing to discuss a settlement to end the war.
Iran conflict
On Iran, Trump has not ruled out new strikes, including at so-called Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.
Europeans, however, are eager to see a resolution and shipping traffic return to normal in the Strait of Hormuz energy transit hub.
Trump allayed some fears by telling CNN it was "highly unlikely" that fighting would resume.
"We certainly cannot afford any military escalation at this point," said Wadephul, adding the G7 talks would "focus on identifying ways to ensure it is indeed avoided".
Rubio warned however there had been "no progress" in talks with Iran, whose demands he said were "simply not just unacceptable but, in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic".

f9b218ae4e3ba578: JERUSALEM: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu called again Monday for a unity government that would keep him in power, a day after opposition rival Gadi Eisenkot was given a mandate to form a coalition.
"A unity government is, simply, a necessity," Netanyahu said in a video posted on social media that ignored President Isaac Herzog on Sunday formally giving Eisenkot the first chance at a government.
Eisenkot's opposition bloc received 48 out of 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's parliament in Oct 27 elections. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats.

But Eisenkot received a majority of recommendations in parties' talks with Herzog. He could rely on Arab-majority parties, which won a record 19 seats after unprecedented voter turnout on anger over racism and marginalisation by Netanyahu's far-right government.
In his video, Netanyahu warned Israelis against what he described as the threat of including Arab-Israelis in a future government.

"You cannot form a government with Hamas supporters, a government that depends on Hamas supporters," Netanyahu said Monday, repeating an often-used scare tactic against Arab-Israeli parties, which he has also accused of election fraud despite a lack of evidence.

The parties deny the charges. Eisenkot faces resistance within the opposition to including Arab-Israeli parties, which could also vote to put him in power without joining the government, leaving it fragile.
Netanyahu said that a unity government around his Likud party should instead include all Zionist parties as well as ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

Avigdor Liberman, a right-wing critic of Netanyahu and leader of the smallest of the core opposition parties, has made clear he opposes any partnership with Israeli-Arabs, questioning their ideology and warning of the political cost.
Liberman has instead courted the ultra-Orthodox, despite his years of criticism of the community over its key demand that its young people remain exempt from mandatory military service.
Liberman met Monday with Eisenkot in a public show of unity.
"Both expressed full confidence in their ability to form a stable government for a full four-year term," Liberman's Yashar party said in a statement.
Eisenkot and Netanyahu have both offered a national-unity government with the rival party -- but with each one insisting he would be in charge.

Eisenkot has publicly said that Netanyahu is dangerous and unfit to lead Israel, pointing to his failure to prevent the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack, his deep divisiveness and corruption charges that could land Netanyahu in prison if he were to lose power.

4fa1ac302282b627: ANTALYA: The COP31 climate talks kicked off Monday with an early fight over money as the UN's chief urged world leaders to "get serious" about tackling the crisis after a year of devastating weather extremes.
Antonio Guterres made his plea as thousands of participants descended on a sprawling expo centre in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya for the UN's annual two-week climate conference.

The summit comes after a year of punishing heatwaves in Europe, major wildfires in Indonesia and catastrophic floods in Nepal, with an exceptionally strong El Nino weather phenomenon fuelling more climate chaos.
Observers expect few major breakthroughs at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war with Iran and Russia's conflict in Ukraine.

In a statement, the UN secretary-general urged leaders to "get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need".

Old battles over money emerged even before COP31 started, with negotiators debating until the early hours of Monday over demands by developing nations to include items on climate finance in the official agenda.

Under UN climate agreements, developed countries, which are historically responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions, have provided financial support to help developing nations adapt to climate impacts and transition to cleaner energy.
Climate finance discussions "will always be a challenge, because it's all about competing priorities", Papua New Guinea's Ruel Yamuna, the COP31 Pacific envoy for climate finance access, told AFP.
"It's like Christmas. You have a long Christmas list ... you want it all but you can't have it all," Yamuna said.

Jasper Inventor, head of Greenpeace's COP31 delegation, said developed countries had taken a "hard line" over whether to include a platform, agreed at COP30 in Brazil last year, aimed at discussing how wealthy nations should provide funds to developing nations.
But it was ultimately added to the agenda.

African countries also unsuccessfully pushed for a specific agenda item on tripling adaptation finance, which aims to help poorer nations pay for measures such as building sea walls or planting drought-resistant crops.
The UN says developing countries will need US$305 billion a year by 2035 to adapt to climate change, nearly 10 times what they currently receive from wealthy nations.
A senior EU official warned last week that there would be "no political will" for extra funding pledges at COP31.

The long-term climate outlook is bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global warming will likely exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement.
"This COP must respond to the overshoot to save countries like mine from disappearance," said Maina Talia, climate minister of the Pacific island of Tuvalu.
Fossil fuel fight
Turkey is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference but raised concerns over how it would work.

But COP31 president Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, and Australian climate minister Chris Bowen hailed their partnership, raising their clasped hands above their heads to applause during the opening ceremony.
The partners have branded the summit as the "implementation COP", focusing on turning commitments into concrete action after years of ambitious announcements.
"We know that delay carries one of the heaviest costs in climate action," Kurum said.
Turkey is inviting countries to join a voluntary "electrification" pledge to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 percent today to 35% by 2035.
'Clean' electrification
The EU has called for "clean" electrification, a term that could spark debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.
Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.

COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language, prompting the Brazilian hosts to propose a voluntary "roadmap" for countries to transition to clean energy.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who will be among leaders addressing COP31 later this week, was due to attend the talks, fresh from a re-election win that activists hailed as a victory for climate change.
But climate diplomacy is still missing a major player as climate-sceptic US President Donald Trump has not sent officials to COP31.
A US congressional delegation, however, will come to Antalya, with Democrats beaming after last week's historic US midterm election win.

1734b025345cf516: On October 19, a unit of Salvadoran soldiers was also ambushed; the situation remains tense
Originally published on Global Voices
View of the hills from the road from Port-au-Prince to Kenscoff. Photo by Ketounette via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

In the heights of Pétion-Ville, more than 1,500 metres above sea level, sits the municipality of Kenscoff. A rural area just 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) southeast of downtown Port-au-Prince, Kenscoff is an idyllic contradiction of sorts. Its breathtaking landscape is dominated by pine trees and mountain ridges, dotted with terraced gardens and agricultural fields that supply fruit, vegetables and flowers to Port-au-Prince markets, grocery chains and restaurants. Yet, because of its high elevation, it can also get very cold and foggy, with the sun often setting by five in the afternoon.

The majority of Kenscoff’s residents are peasant farmers, though some wealthy Haitians, craving more peace, quiet, and fresh air, have chosen to leave the nearby urban areas of Port-au-Prince and Pétion-Ville for the area’s pastoral charm and community spirit.

Kenscoff was famous for hosting recreational events where people would come to spend the day, eat fritay (fried foods), ride horses, and visit Fort Jacques, the area’s main historic site. Visitors would also frequent Ranch le Montcel — now temporarily closed (burned during gang violence in 2025) — and Chalet Le Refuge, a once popular recreational, social and dining centre, now also closed.

But that was a different Kenscoff, before armed gangs attacked the town in two deadly attacks this year — July 7–8 and August 23–24 — burning down houses, killing 164 people, and kidnapping and displacing others. Like many other regions in the country, the Kenscoff community suddenly turned from peaceful daily living into being held to ransom by criminal elements.

It all began about two years ago, when the area began to be disrupted by gangs’ attempts to invade the mountains and establish bases there, foiled by the vigilance of residents’ self-defence brigades, with the help of the Haitian police and army. Yet, every time these attacks occurred, several civilians would be killed, while others abandoned their homes, seeking refuge in the centre of Pétion-Ville, which was less exposed to gang violence.

According to a report by the National Human Rights Defense Network (RNDDH) on the two massacres, the apathy shown by the government and high-ranking security officials, despite warnings, contributed to the scale of the losses.

On September 18, close to a month after the second attack, lawyer, human rights activist and RNDDH Programme Director Rosy Auguste Ducéna detailed what happened during her appearance on the show Se Sa NOU VLE, hosted by Rudy Thomas Sanon on the Team Rudy Officiel YouTube channel.

For its investigation, she said, the RNDDH collected testimonies from various local authorities, including the interim mayor and his deputy chief of staff, the justice of the peace (District judge) and his deputy, the police chief, police officers, members of self-defence brigades, and about 100 victims and their relatives who managed to survive.

But these two massacres were not Kenscoff’s first experience with this type of violence. The town suffered its first attack from January 27 to 29, 2025, forcing many people to flee to the Kenscoff town hall to find shelter. There they stayed until Easter 2026, when the interim mayor relocated them to the Afè Nèg Konbit school in the Robin area, which was considered relatively safe. As the terror of July 7-8 later proved, Ducéna said, this turned out to be a false sense of security:

Jou 7 jiyè 2026 la, popilasyon an rete yo wè bandi yo ap koupe pye bwa, yo itilize pye bwa sa yo pou yo fè barikad, e yo pa konprann poukisa. Se pa la swit lè masak la pral vin pase lannwit 7 pou louvri 8 jiyè, ke yo pral konprann yo te fè barikad sa yo pou te anpeche vehikil blende la polis yo rive nan lokalite Robin. Nan sware 7 pou louvri 8 jiyè sa, yo atake plizyè zòn ki fè pati lokalite Robin.

On July 7, 2026, the population suddenly saw the bandits cutting down trees and using them to build barricades, and they didn’t understand why. It was only after the massacre, which happened during the night of July 7 into July 8, that they realised the bandits built those barricades to prevent police armoured vehicles from reaching the Robin area. During that night, they attacked several zones that are part of Robin.
She added:

Yo touye moun, yo itilize kadav moun yo kòm barikad yo mete bò kote bwa yo te itilize kòm barikad yo tou. Apre sa yo rantre nan kan ki andedan lekòl la, yo tire sou moun, yo boule moun tou vivan, yo touye moun yo pike dife sou kadav yo, yo boule zafè moun yo andedan espas la.

They killed people, and they used the dead bodies as barricades alongside the trees. Then, they went inside the camp at the school. They shot at people, burned people alive, killed people and set their bodies on fire, and burned people’s belongings inside the space.

After this, Ducéna explained, the community tried to recover, but persistent rumours began to spread about another potential attack by the gang led by Didier Chérisme — known as “Didi” or “IZO 2”, a member of the criminal coalition Viv Ansanm.

Rumblings of a planned second massacre grew so strong that on July 27, the head of the Kenscoff police station sent a report to his superiors requesting additional armoured vehicles. The very next day, he sent a second report asking to reinforce the operational capacity of the Kenscoff police station.

Despite these two urgent requests, the Kenscoff station received no logistical or human support, making it easier for the gang to attack the town on August 23–24. Police officers were outnumbered and lacked the vehicles needed to counteract the attack. According to Ducéna, the information that was collected showed that a large-scale massacre was being prepared, “but there was no response — absolutely no response.”

The RNDDH report details that just a few days before the massacre, the police high command had reduced the number of officers assigned to Kenscoff by nearly 60 percent. They also reduced the number of armoured vehicles available to the station.

Meanwhile, days before the massacre, the bandits infiltrated the area with the help of certain locals. They also used surveillance drones to monitor the movements of the community and track the presence of law enforcement. The attack started around 10:00 p.m. on the night of August 23 and continued into the following day as gang members surrounded downtown Kenscoff, making their way through several neighbourhoods before entering the town centre.

As they moved, they committed multiple atrocities and created distractions to make the police believe they were attacking several areas at once. This forced officers to intervene in different places every time the gangs carried out a quick attack. This made it easier for the bandits to infiltrate the heart of downtown.
As Ducéna concluded:
Sa vle di n ap pale la ke bandi yo ap fè se de operasyon ki byen kalkile, byen chapante, byen prepare.
This means we are talking about operations by the bandits that are well-calculated, well-structured, and well-prepared.

Once the gangs reached the immediate vicinity of the police station and the Kenscoff town hall, the situation began to deteriorate significantly. “From that moment on,” Ducéna noted, “they unleashed violence against the population of Kenscoff. People’s age, gender, disabilities, or vulnerability did not stop them in their rage and their desire to kill people at all costs.”

The nightmare continued that night when the attackers entered the L'Âge de la Nouvelle Alliance church, which had been serving as a shelter for people who had already been displaced by previous massacres. Ducéna is convinced that the gang knew people had taken refuge there, and many atrocities were committed. Just as with the July massacre, gang members killed residents, injured and burned others alive, raped women and young girls, and burned down houses, cars and motorcycles.

The slaughter continued until about 3:00 a.m., when a group of police officers and vigilance committee members intervened and limited any further damage. Despite being forced to retreat, however, the gangs kidnapped more than 60 people, including women, young girls, babies, and the sick and elderly.

A few days later, through mediation by a citizen named Luckson Jean (also known as “Frè Luckson”), who runs a children’s center, and the support of UNICEF, several children and babies were released. However, dozens of people are still being held hostage under constant threat of execution, should the police intervene.

A few days after the massacre in Kenscoff, the Haitian National Police (PNH), with armoured vehicles and the private military company Vertus Global owned by Erik Prince, carried out operations to clear the area of armed gangs using helicopters and drones. According to a report by the Haitian National Police, six hostages were released, and several gang members were seriously injured or killed. However, the police have not yet provided any information about the other people who were taken hostage. For now, life in Kenscoff is slowly returning to normal, but fear remains in people’s minds.
In and around the metropolitan area of Port-au-Prince, the security situation remains dangerous, particularly in the commune of Croix-des-Bouquets, to the northeast of Port-au-Prince.

f30dc75a69e1f122: Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship.
Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments.

“Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions.
Neither AWS nor Qubole responded to The Register's inquiries.

Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles.

The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872, and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS, Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote.
This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account.
Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store.

The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments.

Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data.
The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data.

While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity.
Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued.

Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses.

“For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.”®

2969b0807146033c: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.
Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.
But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

15f1bb7e65192a16: Security researchers exploited flaws in Android apps to gain remote access to connected cars from two major automakers, allowing them to start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns.

Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year. By tinkering with the cars’ Android apps, they devised exploit paths to issue remote commands to vehicles in Australia and the US.

The pair published separate blogs covering different aspects of the research; Shah said the US attack "required a lot more work" because the automaker "spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments."

Both exploit chains centered around weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity platform relied upon by both automakers, the identities of which were kept anonymous by the researchers, who have previously highlighted flaws in the likes of Hyundai, Kia, Subaru, and many others.

In the Australian version of the app, the researchers first found a vehicle identification number (VIN) using public licence plate checkers, and used those in queries to internal APIs, which provided personal information and owner email addresses.

They also found hardcoded admin credentials for the ForgeRock OpenIDM that were meant for the staging environment but also worked in production. After bypassing the heavy WAF filtering by exploiting path traversal flaws, they were able to invoke the internal admin APIs and take over target accounts using only their email addresses.
This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send arbitrary commands to affected vehicles through the mobile app.

Issuing commands on the US version also required bypassing WAF filtering through a path traversal, though with a more involved technique: exploiting path confusion to reach the Apache Felix admin console.

The researchers used factory default credentials in Felix’s OSGi Web Console to gain admin privileges. They then used Felix configuration manager to schedule a task that executed an inline Groovy script, giving them shell access to the identity servers.

The researchers then queried local admin API endpoints, allowing them to view or modify user account data. From there, they logged into car owners’ accounts, and gained the ability to issue the same commands as demonstrated in the Australian version.
According to Curry’s disclosure timeline, he and Shah approached the affected automakers in "early 2026," and the exploits were patched within two hours of receiving the report.

Although the automakers wished to remain anonymous, it didn’t take long for some petrolheads to speculate that the partially blurred car in Shah’s demo video was a Toyota, citing the shape of the wing mirror and the unlock sound it made.

Onlookers claimed that the two automakers in question were likely Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus. Asked wether the claims were accurate, a spokesperson for Toyota Motor Corporation neither confirmed nor denied them.
Curry said he and Shah chose to uphold the manufacturers’ requests to remain anonymous out of concern for infoseccers’ current workloads.

He said: "Obviously, they have asked not to be named, and while normally we would fight to actually include the company names, it's a busy time in the security world and I don't like the idea of them diverting resources because they are worried about something with this disclosure." ®

1f917ef42e116f1b: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.

The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.

This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.

da795f2924119e2e: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

“It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”

Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”

Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”

Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says.

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”

Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.”

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

cdba77295d09f210: Investors, especially the financial press, spend a lot of time trying to explain what just happened. The problem is that this exercise is filled with hindsight bias, causal assumptions, and narrative fallacy that don’t withstand scrutiny.
Last week was a perfect example of that. I want to take a contrarian view of what happened Thursday to suss out what we do and don’t know, and what might have been driving all of the volatility.
1. The Sell-Off

Thursday was one of the most significant one-day sell-offs we have seen in a long while. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12%, with some names like SanDisk, AMD, Micron, and Marvell falling much more. Reuters noted it was the second-worst day for semiconductors on record.

The S&P 500 fell 4.4% — the worst drop since the tariffs announcement in April 2025 (“Liberation Day”). The Nasdaq, which had hit an all-time high in October, fell ~12% below that mark. The Volatility Index reflected this; the VIX saw its third-largest percentage jump ever, gaining 69.7% as it leaped from 16 to over 28.

Perhaps most significant was Nvidia, which is now negative for the year. The heaviest weight in the S&P 500, it fell 9.3% that day. How widely known Jensen Huang’s now-publicized affair with a Chinese Spy is undetermined.1
2. Unlikely Causes

The “Blunami”, a Democratic landslide victory on Tuesday, was well understood early election night (November 3rd), well before midnight. Despite the substantial rally the day after the election, a new narrative began by the end of Thursday.

This was all known on the day after the election (Wednesday, November 4th). It was a historically strong post-midterm election rally. Markets rose, and if you want a theory why, there were plenty: anticipation of an end to the Iran war, lower gas prices, lower inflation – maybe even future rate cuts. Of course, congressional gridlock is always a winning theme.

President Trump also surprised people by accepting the election outcome. The historical thumping was so great, it would have been laughable to claim otherwise. Whatever the reason, it led to the market’s best day in three months.

Thursday more than erased those gains, yet nothing new emerged from the election results. Indeed, markets rallied hard the next day (Friday) and, despite the Jensen Huang/Nvidia news, were up strongly at noon today.

No significant political news emerged between late Tuesday night and now. This makes the dominant AP storyline look like a lazy narrative fallacy, an attempt to fit the results into a superficial storyline. The AP timeline makes no sense and strongly suggests the dominant Associated Press narrative is bullshit.
3. Three Possible Causes
Several potential drivers of the selloff resonate more with me than the political narrative.

The first was rumors about a forced liquidation of data center loans. Bloomberg covered one side of the story mid-day: “Mystery Seller Puts Up $500 Million Data Center Loans”; this aligns with a reversal in bullish sentiment. The next day, it was revealed that the seller was ING.2
Given the hundreds of billions already invested by the hyperscalers in the AI data center buildout, half a billion dollars is a modest sum and should not be enough debt to cause widespread panic.
While I do not believe this was the cause, sometimes, all it takes to ignite a room full of flammable gas is a small spark.

The second possible culprit was the rebalancing of the (too) popular leveraged ETFs of an estimated $50 billion.3 Dave Nadig of ETF.com puts the daily rebal at ~$58 billion; he notes this does not include flow, and that the day’s volatility adds to the magnitude (but is agnostic about the direction). The ETF rebal was more likely a result of the sell-off, and not an underlying cause.

The third potential cause – and in my mind, the most significant – was a huge, leveraged growth unwind by the major multi-strategy hedge funds. These pod shops are filled with quants who frequently end up in crowded trades – this time, it was semiconductors and AI.

Rumors circulated that ~108 separate pods closed and unwound on Thursday in what is best described as “forced liquidations.” That might help explain the fastest $2.5 trillion wipeout on record. (Note we saw a somewhat less ugly selloff on the last trading day of October).

For those unfamiliar with the term “pod shops,” these are multi-manager, multi-strategy hedge funds that have hundreds of small, semi-autonomous trading teams – aka “pods” – on the same platform. Many of the best-known multi-strat funds run large amounts of capital: Millennium ($98B), Citadel ($77B), Point72 ($55.5B), Balyasny ($37B), Schonfeld Strategic Advisors ($23.5B), Hudson Bay Capital ($20B), etc. Add to that Viking and many other Tiger shops, and it all adds up to a rather sizeable amount of capital.

The strategies may differ, but one consistent theme is centralized risk management that aggregates all positions across every pod’s book in real time. Last Thursday felt (at least to me) like many of these pods got caught in a crowded, systematic,long-leveraged growth equity trade. Think mega-cap growth, momentum, and tech names, especially AI/Semis.

The multi-strat shops are disciplined, mechanical, and formulaic. Any pod that hits a specific drawdown limit triggers a hard stop automatically. When I refer to forced liquidation, this is precisely what I mean.4

Can you tell in advance when a sell-off might occur? As the market trends upward, the leverage doesn’t get much notice. I would surmise it is close to impossible to guess when quakes of this sort might occur or when you can sound the all-clear whistle. We never really know just how crowded a trade might be until the unwind. (See JPM report at right as a counter-example of the dangers of assuming it was safe).

My bet is that Citadel Securities and Jane Street were the counterparties to a massive unwind, similar to the Situational Awareness trade over the summer. We will find out if that suspicion is true as soon as rumors of windfall trading profits in November for those two firms begin to circulate.

Was the catalyst political? I highly doubt it; Wednesday’s rally was long after the Blue Tsunami was understood. The much more likely cause was forced liquidations of a crowded quant/momentum trade driven by tightly run risk management at pod shops.

Cliff Asness explained a decade after the 2007 Quant Quake, “Crashes are runs on the bank and it’s very hard, even for genius physicists, to predict social panic, let alone the magnitude of one versus another.”
Some lessons from those experiences apparently became systematic trading rules, too…
