70bbc1169fd03a37: Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave.

World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes.

Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus."

The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom "nature makes no leaps," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference.

Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time."

Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action.

But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted.

Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions.
Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur.

"In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were.
"Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction."
Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements.

"The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained. "Those two meters are the signature of the current that occurred. To answer 'where would the boat be had I steered right?', we take the world model's prediction for steering right and add the same two meters. In other words, the counterfactual is what actually happened, plus the difference between the model's predictions for the alternative action and for the action taken.

"Physics enters to justify this rule, not as an equation the model fits. Over a short time, the effect of the action and the effect of the current each grow in proportion to the duration, while their interaction grows only with its square, so over short steps they simply add up, like forces.

"We prove that the fraction of the disturbance's effect that this rule gets wrong shrinks with the square of the time step, and that no method using the same ordinary data can do better than this rate in the worst case."
Counterfactual world models have three likely uses, according to Balestriero. The first is having a robot retry an action after a surprise event.

"When an attempt fails because of something the robot could not see, such as an unexpected load, a current or a weak motor, the counterfactual world model lets it estimate which action would have worked in that same situation," he explained. "In our simulated tasks, choosing the action this way reaches the goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner that knows the true simulator but ignores the observed outcome. With two more attempts on the same event, success rises to 51 to 97 percent."
He also sees these models being useful for adapting to persistent fault, like a miscalibrated motor, and helping people understand failures.

"World models are trained to predict, and they are getting good at it," said Balestriero. "But a robot, a car or a drone acting in the real world is constantly surprised by things it could not see coming. After a surprise, the useful question is no longer what was expected, but what would have happened had it acted differently in that same situation. You need that answer to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, or to decide what to do on the next attempt, and prediction alone does not provide it."

The researchers initial attempts to address the issue involved adding a learned component to the world model that infers whatever hidden disturbance (e.g. the current in the boat scenario) affected the anticipated outcome. But that approach was too fragile.

"Trying to understand why led to the theory," explained Balestriero. "Learning the disturbance from ordinary data is not just hard, it is impossible in general: the hidden noise can be relabeled differently for each action without changing a single prediction, so the data cannot tell you which labeling is the right one. The missing piece has to come from outside the data. For physical systems, it comes from the fact that forces add and that their interaction builds up slowly in time. Once you accept that, the learned disturbance model becomes unnecessary: the gap between what happened and what was predicted already carries the information you need, and you carry it over to the other action."
Balestriero said that control engineers have been implementing corrections of this sort for decades, to tune hand-built models.

"What was missing was why the same correction is justified for learned world models that see the world through images, what can and cannot be recovered without paired data, and where it breaks," he said. "The paper answers these questions by connecting causal inference, control and world models. The title comes from Leibniz's law of continuity, natura non facit saltus, 'nature makes no leaps,' which is precisely the property that makes all of this work."
The researchers' paper was provided to The Register prior to its release on ArXiv. It is expected to be released this week. ®

6f2117f6f58d050d: Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings.

It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter.

Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior.

However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again.
Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up.

You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently.
It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to reach the dialog.
Former Microsoft engineer Charles Opperman said he wrote the dialog in early 1995 "after @bradsilverberg kids kept activating StickeyKeys [sic] while playing Space Cadet pinball."

Opperman added that a link to Settings was added in Windows 98 or what would become Windows 2000, and a checkbox was considered even then, but it wasn't deemed a priority. Users could turn off the prompt via settings. Now the option is front and center.
The option is also rolling out in the Windows Insider Beta channel, although Microsoft has not announced a general release date. ®

87e382549731171b: PARIS: French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu on Monday said the government would raise the minimum wage slightly in response to cost-of-living protests, but unions swiftly dismissed the offer as "crumbs".

Protesters in the eurozone's second-largest economy have in recent weeks demanded higher wages, but the government has limited leeway to respond as it seeks to rein in high deficit and debt ahead of presidential elections next year.
After meeting the unions, Lecornu promised to increase the minimum wage by 1.6% on Dec 1.
That would include an adjustment for inflation of 1% and an extra boost of 0.6%, he said.
This would raise the minimum wage by around €24 to around €1,502 net per month – far below that demanded by the unions.
The CFDT had called for a €100 increase and the CGT for around €150.
CFDT general secretary Marylise Leon said that the proposed hike was "insufficient".
CGT leader Sophie Binet dismissed the extra five euros a month on top of the automatic adjustment for inflation anyway as "crumbs".
"Five euros is one kilo of tomatoes," she said.
France adjusts its minimum wage for inflation every January. The last discretionary boost dates back to 2012.
Public sector unions have called for a strike and demonstrations on Nov 17.
1a04107834027bb8: NASA is moving ahead with its plan to repurpose a Mars rover engineering model as a lunar trundlebot for less than $400 million.

The robot, dubbed PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), is a cut-and-shut of engineering test articles used for the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers, currently rolling around the Red Planet.

During a weekend briefing, NASA outlined the plan for PROMISE: to land the robot on the lunar surface by late 2028 for an 18-month mission. PROMISE will be preceded by NASA's VIPER trundlebot, which is expected to survive only 100 days on the Moon's surface. PROMISE will carry copies of VIPER's science instruments, including a drill capable of boring 1 meter into the lunar regolith.

Power will come from a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) left over from the Cassini mission. NASA acknowledged the fuel was processed some time ago – the Cassini mission to Saturn was launched in 1997 – but anticipates there will be plenty of heat and power for PROMISE's components.

Blue Origin is to deposit the rover on the Moon. NASA awarded the company a $94 million base contract, "with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole."

The figures make it difficult to ascertain the exact cost of the PROMISE mission. However, during the briefing, NASA said it had "a pretty firm agreement with JPL to basically deliver the rover to the surface under $400 million." The $400 million includes the lander, which will be Blue Origin's Mark 1.

Earlier this year, The Planetary Society's chief of space policy, Casey Drier, estimated that the mission (including repurposing the hardware developed for Mars and landing it on the Moon) would cost at least $723 million. At the time, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said: "if PROMISE costs even 20 percent of your low-end estimate, we simply will not fly it."
Assuming Isaacman was only talking about the rover, Drier's figure drops to $489 million without launch and landing costs. 20 percent of that is… not going to be enough.

That also doesn't account for the impact of taking away the hardware built for the Mars program. During the briefing, NASA said it was "pretty comfortable" with how the Mars rovers were going and so was happy about repurposing the hardware or, as one speaker put it, "can we give it a new paint job?"

A source told The Register that morale at the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) was not high at present. Raiding successful programs to fulfill the administration's whims is unlikely to have improved the mood of engineers.
Still. Another trundlebot on the Moon. Far better than using that spare RTG for yet another deep space mission, right? ®

8078a93fa169cba3: ALOR STAR: A speech by Kedah's fifth Menteri Besar, Datuk Seri Syed Nahar Syed Sheh Shahabuddin, delivered nearly 47 years ago, has been transcribed from an audio recording, shedding light on a little-known chapter of the state's history during the Japanese occupation.
The speech was delivered on Dec 14, 1979, at the commemorative stone-laying ceremony for Kampung Lindungan Raja in Sedim, Kulim.
It recounts historical events in Sedim during the Japanese occupation, including how the late Sultan Abdul Hamid was given refuge in the village.
The transcription was completed on Oct 25 by Malaysian Historical Society Kedah branch chairman Syamsyul Anuar Ismail, who retained every word as recorded in the original audio.
"The audio recording is still kept by the Malaysian Historical Society Kedah branch. The language used is the everyday spoken dialect of the Kedah community," he said.

Syamsyul, who is also a senior lecturer at Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM), said the speech was historically significant as Syed Nahar recounted the origins of Kampung Lindungan Raja, which were closely linked to events when Japanese forces invaded Malaya in 1941.
The speech also recalled how the late Sultan Abdul Hamid was taken to Sedim for refuge after his journey to Penang was blocked by Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra Al-Haj and several companions.
"One of the interesting accounts in the speech was how Tunku Abdul Rahman and several of his companions stopped the late Sultan Abdul Hamid from travelling to Penang.
"At the time, the Sultan was travelling to seek refuge at the request of the British authorities following the advance of Japanese forces in Malaya," he said.
Syamsyul said that, according to the account, the Sultan was taken from Bumbung Lima to Kulim before being brought safely to Sedim on Dec 12, 1941.
"This event also reflects the loyalty of Sedim residents, who were willing to shelter the Sultan when Malaya was under threat from Japanese forces.
"Syed Nahar himself stated in the speech that he was still a young child and living in Sedim when the incident took place," he said.
Syamsyul said the transcription was important to preserve the recording's contents in written form and make them available as historical reference material, particularly on Kedah's history.

9f0586a8b801e2f1: PETALING JAYA: DAP's legal bureau chairman Ramkarpal Singh has defended the Attorney-General's Chambers' position on the court order concerning Najib Razak’s house arrest, saying it does not amount to questioning the king's prerogative in granting pardons.

"As such, clarification of the said Order of Discharge is necessary to avoid any doubts which may arise in the enforcement of the said conditional pardon order.

Third-seeded Magda Linette of Poland rallied past top-seeded Janice Tjen of Indonesia to win the title in Chennai, India, taking the final 5-7, 6-1, 6-4 on Monday morning.

6b71eb9713c14243: In sports, a “dead rubber” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty.

A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1.

Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. More disruption came from grid penalties for Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, both of whom needed to use extra power unit components outside of the season’s allowance.

d5182c22841e1d44: NEW YORK: Technology share prices clawed back some of last week's sharp losses on Monday, though gains were tempered by a plunge in Nvidia following a probe into its boss Jensen Huang over claims of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Oil prices fell 5% on hopes for diplomatic talks aimed at ending the US-Iran war.

Chipmakers and other companies linked to the artificial intelligence boom took a hammering in the days after last Tuesday's US midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep both chambers of Congress, leading to speculation lawmakers would seek to rein in tech firms.
But Wall Street's main indices opened higher, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq adding 0.9%.
Briefing.com analyst Patrick O'Hare said the rebound in equities was due to more than just the drop in oil prices.
"What we also have this morning is an inclination to buy into last week's weakness, and specifically into the large losses seen in the AI trade," he said in a note to clients.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which includes major chipmakers and AI firms, rose 1.9%.
But the gains did not extend to Nvidia, which saw its shares slump more than eight percent as trading got underway in New York.
O'Hare said Nvidia was being treated as a one-off story by investors for the moment.

"In other words, the stock is being penalised for Jensen Huang's personal transgression, which has invited a great deal of uncertainty into the mix, but the market isn't caught up in the notion that this situation is going to have a systemic domino effect," he said.

The news that Nvidia's board would investigate whether Huang had been targeted in a foreign espionage plot, following his admission he was unfaithful to his wife, brought fresh uncertainty in the markets.

The New York Times last month reported that US intelligence officials concluded a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed had been funnelling information to Beijing.
The executive, Alice Huang – also known as Huang Le, and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Jensen – developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the Times said.
In a message to company employees released to media on Sunday, Huang acknowledged having an affair and apologised to his family and company staff.

Nvidia is a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models and one of the world's most valuable companies, and last year became the first to reach a market capitalisation of US$5 trillion.

Technology analyst Dan Ives, at the investment bank Yorkville Ives, said the crisis would at the very least spark congressional inquiries and "create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons".
"This will add risk to the stock, as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally," Ives said.
"This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC," he added.
China on Monday said the claims that it had spied on Huang were "baseless".
Europe's main stock markets rose in afternoon trading following gains across much of Asia.
The dollar fell against its main rivals.

2f569ab9a556da2b: THE midterms have shifted the balance of power in Washington, but whether they will alter American foreign policy is an open question. For Malaysia and its neighbours, that distinction carries real consequences.

Democrats have won control of both houses of Congress but we need to be mindful of cliched references about President Donald Trump being therefore "politically hamstrung" for his remaining two-year "lame duck" period.

At first blush, congressional control by the Democrats may constrain Trump at home but let us not forget he is still the president and one who wields significant veto powers. It offers little reason to expect a more predictable or accommodating US.

American policy is increasingly shaped by forces that do not always pull in the same direction. Some reflect Trump's personal instincts and negotiating style. Others command support across party lines and are likely to outlast his presidency. The rest of us will need to tell the two apart.

Undoubtedly, the scale of the Republican defeat was striking. Democrats made gains even in traditionally conservative states, a result of anger over living costs, the war with Iran and Trump's conduct in office. His devoted supporters could not sustain the broader coalition that returned him to the White House in 2024, and two years later enough voters were ready to punish his party.

The Democratic victory should nonetheless be kept in proportion. Divided government is hardly unusual in American history, and Trump governed with a Democratic House during the final two years of his first term without showing much deference to Congress.

The incoming Congress can investigate the administration, challenge spending decisions and obstruct legislation. Democratic control of the Senate will complicate presidential appointments. Trump, meanwhile, retains substantial executive powers and his veto. Democrats lack the numbers to override the latter or to secure his removal from office following impeachment. Nevertheless, War Secretary Peter Hegseth will most likely be thrown under the bus to appease the bloodthirsty group braying for his pound of flesh, metaphorically speaking.

Washington may become consumed by partisan confrontation, with little to show in substantive policy. For America's trading partners, whose interests rarely feature prominently in domestic political battles, that prospect offers scant comfort.

Trade illustrates the difficulty. Democrats have criticised Trump's tariffs for raising costs for American businesses and consumers, and some restrictions may now face closer scrutiny. Economic nationalism has also taken root in both major parties. Protecting domestic manufacturing, resisting Chinese competition and using trade to advance strategic goals all enjoy considerable bipartisan support.

For Malaysia, the more consequential question is how far American trade policy has become an instrument of strategic competition. Tariffs may change, but it would be naive to expect any pushback in the use of economic leverage against trading partners.

The stakes for advanced technology may be higher. Competition with China over semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI) commands broad support in Washington. Senator Chris Coons, who is expected to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has called for an investigation into alleged connections involving Chinese intelligence and leading figures in the American AI industry. This was on the cards even before the Financial Times expose of Nvidia's Jensen Huang affair with Alice Huang, allegedly a Chinese intelligence operative. If indeed a spy, that would be the oldest trick in the book. Congressional pressure on Trump over China could therefore intensify.

Malaysia is particularly exposed here. Its semiconductor industry and expanding data centre sector have made it an important participant in global technology supply chains, and they have also drawn American scrutiny over the possibility that restricted equipment could reach China through intermediaries.

A more assertive Congress could press for tighter export controls, closer checks on end users and stronger enforcement against suspected diversion. Access to advanced American technologies may depend increasingly on satisfying US regulatory and security requirements.
Malaysia has legitimate commercial interests with both the US and China, and protecting them will require credible enforcement, clear regulation and sustained engagement with both countries.

Relations between Washington and Beijing may grow more complicated for much the same reason. Trump has shown a willingness to negotiate directly with President Xi Jinping, at times pursuing arrangements that diverge from the wider American strategic consensus. After his domestic setback, he may have stronger incentives to secure deals offering economic relief or a visible diplomatic success.

An understanding between the two presidents would leave many underlying disputes unresolved. Congress could challenge concessions involving sensitive technologies or security commitments, and American regulators would retain considerable influence over implementation. Like the rest of us, Beijing must now deal with an administration whose priorities may differ from those of other powerful institutions in Washington.

For Southeast Asia, these competing pressures complicate an already difficult relationship with Washington. Vietnam and Thailand remain exposed to American trade restrictions through their manufacturing sectors. Singapore's weight in finance and advanced technology brings different sensitivities, and Indonesia's ambitions in critical minerals and industrial development may meet American objections. The Philippines must contend with questions about the reliability of American security commitments amid tensions over Taiwan and the South China Sea.

These differences make a common Asean response difficult. The region nonetheless shares an interest in strengthening its own economic foundations and reducing vulnerabilities that outside powers can exploit. Regional integration remains incomplete, and the growing use of economic restrictions for strategic purposes makes it more pressing.

The war with Iran adds another source of uncertainty. It contributed heavily to Trump's electoral difficulties by driving up energy prices and household costs. His administration now faces competing pressures to negotiate an end to the conflict or resume major military operations, and Congress may have limited ability to determine the outcome.

For Malaysia, the immediate concern is the effect on energy supplies, shipping and global demand. As an energy producer, Malaysia has some advantages, but higher freight costs and inflation would still burden businesses and households. A prolonged conflict would also weigh on the wider Asian economy.

The election also produced a milestone. Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan, making him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, is pivotal in its own right. The Islamophobic attacks directed against him during the campaign, though, were a troubling reminder of the prejudices that persist in American political life.

As for the congressional stance on Israel, any suggestion of a major shift is wishful thinking. While progressive factions are up in arms against Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries over their alignment with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee having benefited from the financial largesse heaped on them, chances are they will continue to lead in Congress, on account of the deep institutional backing within the party.

Trump's defeat does not mean the forces that brought him to power have disappeared. His successors may keep much of his approach to trade, immigration and relations with China, and even a future Democratic president would face strong pressure to protect American industries and maintain technological advantages over strategic rivals.

For Malaysia, the practical implication is clear. We must deal with the US as it is. Washington remains an indispensable economic and diplomatic partner, but effective engagement means working with Congress, regulatory agencies and the wider political currents shaping American policy.

This also calls for greater investment in our own capabilities. A country that depends heavily on foreign technology, markets and investment cannot insulate itself from decisions made elsewhere. Sound institutions, regulatory credibility and a more competitive economy can give us greater room to manoeuvre.

The midterms are a setback for Trump and an affirmation of American democratic accountability. For Asia, the consequences are less clear. The balance of power in Washington has shifted, but the forces behind American economic nationalism and strategic competition with China have not gone away.
Datuk Prof Dr Mohd Faiz Abdullah is Executive Chairman of the Institute
of Strategic and International Studies, Malaysia.

01962daaac78eb1a: THE seasons are unchanging; the hot, dry season is always followed by the wet season. What changes is the country's landscape: verdant lands where forests and crops coexist will increasingly give way to urbanisation as the pace of development quickens.

This means the natural landscape and its capacity to absorb rainfall will inexorably give way to paved and concreted cityscapes, where only adequate drainage systems can spare us from inevitable floods during the rainy season or even the occasional heavy thunderstorm.

Thus, it is high time the country stopped treating floods as a seasonal emergency requiring temporary fixes and instead focused on the structural and environmental factors that make flooding a recurring problem year in, year out.
Social activist Tan Sri Lee Lam Thye has a point when he says Malaysia must move beyond repeated drain-clearing exercises and adopt a long-term flood mitigation strategy.
The country's ageing drainage infrastructure, as well as woefully inadequate drainage systems in most towns and cities, needs an overall review.
What is clearly needed is a comprehensive overhaul to address ageing or inadequate drainage systems, not another round of maintenance and superficial servicing whenever the monsoon approaches.
The National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma) has previously outlined strategies and preparedness measures ahead of the monsoon season.

However, these are largely aimed at managing the consequences of floods as they occur rather than preventing them in the first place. Preparedness is important and necessary, for sure. But it cannot substitute for longer-term solutions.

Those tasked with flood control must resist the reflexive urge to repeat the cycle of reactive responses. Clearing drains and desilting waterways are routine and necessary maintenance exercises. They should, however, be only part of a sustained programme, not the be-all and end-all of the response to flooding.
Systemic weaknesses in the drainage network must be identified and addressed. A serious study is needed to ascertain whether our ageing infrastructure is adequate to address flooding.

This must include a comprehensive assessment of drainage systems, particularly in urban and flood-prone areas. Drainage capacity must keep pace with population growth, urbanisation and increasingly frequent episodes of intense rainfall.

Uncontrolled development, poor land-use planning, the loss of natural water catchment areas, inadequate retention ponds and deforestation all contribute to the problem and must be addressed holistically, not piecemeal.

There must be better coordination across the board, from the federal level down to state and local levels, with clear delineation of responsibilities, implementation timelines and adequate funding for approved mitigation projects.

The end goal must be clear to all: invest in flood prevention, not just recovery efforts. The economic and social costs of repeated flooding — damage to homes, businesses, infrastructure and livelihoods — make a strong case for sustained investment in flood prevention, which will reduce and ultimately eliminate the recurring need for flood recovery efforts.
6bde49fb24c14d3b: BENGALURU: Alphabet's Google introduced two new variations of its in-house tensor processing units (TPUs) on Monday, stepping up its challenge to Nvidia's dominance in the booming artificial intelligence chip market.

The 8tx is aimed at government agencies and companies in regulated industries that need to keep sensitive data protected while it is being processed.

It pairs Google's chip technology with AMD's processors and encrypts data at the hardware level, delivering up to twice the speed of the previous version with virtually no trade-off in performance, the company said.
The 8i Max, meanwhile, is designed for AI applications that need to process very large amounts of information at once.

It combines two chips into a single package to provide additional memory and computing power, the company said, making it well suited to coding assistants, mathematical reasoning and drug discovery tasks.

950f1f8b6bbd8c4b: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking.

Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on.

Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release.
The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1.

There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident, tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another.

Container infrastructure gets plenty of attention, too, with fixes spanning KubeVirt, containerd, Docker Compose, and other components used to keep cloud workloads running. Several CVEs crop up repeatedly across these packages, helping explain the eye-watering number of entries in the changelog.

The release includes less security-focused changes too, including new Dockerfiles, an OpenVMM patch for confidential computing support, fixes for systemd hangs, and adjustments to GRUB Secure Boot metadata.

The hefty release comes amid an AI-fueled surge in vulnerability discovery that has left developers struggling to keep up with the resulting patch workload. As The Register reported earlier today, Linux creator Linus Torvalds reckons there may finally be signs that the flood is easing, at least in some corners of the kernel.

Torvalds said fixes are now arriving faster than new bug reports in the kernel's eBPF subsystem, although he noted that most other areas haven't reached that point. Whether the wider software industry is anywhere close to catching up is another matter, and Microsoft hasn't said if AI-assisted research contributed to the vulnerabilities addressed in this release.

Azure Linux, formerly known as CBL-Mariner, is Microsoft's own Linux distribution, developed primarily for its cloud infrastructure and services. That makes keeping its many components patched rather more important than the modest version-number bump might suggest.
And judging by the size of this latest changelog, Microsoft's patching teams aren't likely to be putting their feet up anytime soon. ®

9c1f0e3e932f0b16: LONDON: Comedian Russell Brand, once one of Britain's most high-profile broadcasters and a Hollywood star, was jailed for 10-and-a-half years on Monday after he was convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three more around two decades ago.

Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question.
"We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse.

Canadian customers, meanwhile, appear to have escaped this particular toilet emergency, with the supplier reporting that no personal information belonging to shoppers in the country was accessed.

Who Gives A Crap says it has since disconnected the provider from its systems, changed access credentials, and begun warning affected customers to watch out for suspicious emails, texts, calls, and other unsolicited communications.
"The main concern is scam or phishing messages that use your real details to look convincing," the company warned in its customer email.

While Who Gives A Crap has been busy cleaning up, the supplier at the center of this particular stink remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified the software provider or disclosed how many customers were affected, including those in the UK, and didn’t respond to our questions.

Griffiths said the company is "engaging with the relevant regulatory authorities, as required." In the UK, the ICO told The Register: "We can confirm Who Gives A Crap Limited has reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided."
Who Gives A Crap has plenty of toilet paper to hand, although cleaning up this particular situation might require more than a few rolls. ®

92c7545f4c38de01: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices.

Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash.
"Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins.

"About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs."
Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare.

Its latest report, "An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register, have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use.

At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources of value.

A recent report from management consultants Bain & Company came to similar conclusions, estimating the AI industry needs to generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding all the infrastructure it needs, and this will require new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity.

Forrester also claims that the forces making AI abundant also make parts of the market unstable, and says that enterprise users should take heed of how prices collapsed as major providers like Anthropic slashed token costs in response to competition from open source models.

If demand disappoints as new capacity comes online, suppliers could cut investment, merge, change prices, or discontinue products. Customers could find themselves rebuilding AI plans around suppliers and services that no longer exist.
Forrester advises businesses to track whether their AI projects deliver measurable value and limit their exposure to vulnerable suppliers – with its help, of course.

Companies can judge how things are going by looking at the gap between suppliers' contracted business and revenue actually recognized, along with how they fund their build-outs. If a vendor leans more on outside investment and customer prepayments, as Oracle and CoreWeave have, this is a red flag to cut back dependencies on them, Forrester says.

Enterprises should also stress-test AI plans against scenarios such as a key vendor announcing end of support in 12 months, and an AI model supplier defaulting on payments to its compute vendor and cutting back service-level agreements for enterprise workloads. Companies should know in advance which AI use cases to drop, what data and workloads need to be moved, and at what cost.

But Hopkins sounded a further note of caution: "Oversupply on its own won't decide whether a correction comes. Demand will, and that's the biggest unknown, because it depends on enterprises finding lasting value in AI beyond simple productivity gains."

Organizations shouldn't pull back, he insists. They should keep investing where AI delivers value that can be demonstrated, closely monitor the financial health of the companies building AI computing, and be ready for corrections.
Recently, the International Monetary Fund started ringing alarm bells that financial markets are increasingly exposed to an AI-driven correction that could lead to widespread economic disruption.

Earlier this year, the Bank for International Settlements also raised concerns that the current situation with the AI industry bore the hallmarks of historical economic bubbles and presented a risk to global economic stability. ®

fb2a8a274448308b: Protesters on Nov. 5 burn a effigy depicting now ex-President Santiago Pena outside Congress in Asuncion, Paraguay, days after the beginning of a banking crisis to which he was linked. AP Photo/Jorge SaenzIt started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money. In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes. The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development. Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs. As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political, economic and environment development, we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability. A bank that grew faster than scrutiny Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers, an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices. As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “Dubai of South America,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers, particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision. But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem. Congress President Basilio Núñez places the presidential sash on Pedro Alliana as he takes office as Paraguay’s new president on Nov. 6, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds. That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure. In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions. The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028. Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “stealing” their savings. When the regulator knows the regulated Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay. Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions. Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term. Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding, which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings, an indirect shareholder in the bank. Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025. Peña has denied any wrongdoing, while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision. The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately $850 million in public funds, including $355 million from the country’s social security system, IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio. Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least $2.3 million in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest. Together these ties and regulatory changes raise important questions about regulatory capture and other potential conflicts of interest. What the growth figures leave out Paraguay’s economic gains are real. In August, the International Monetary Fund projected 4.4% growth in 2026 following 6.6% in 2025. Moody’s granted the country’s debt investment-grade status in 2024, and S&P followed in 2025. Hydroelectric power exports, agriculture and new infrastructure continue to underpin the economy. Demonstrators burn Ueno bank cards during a protest after Paraguay’s central bank took over the bank amid a solvency crisis on Nov. 5, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz Washington is also drawing Paraguay more firmly into its regional economic strategy. On Oct. 23, the country became the 26th signatory to the Pax Silica Declaration, an initiative involving critical minerals, hydropower and advanced computing infrastructure. While the announcement did not specify financing commitments, it shows how Paraguay’s resources and perceived political predictability are being positioned as strategic assets. But growth figures and credit ratings say little about who shapes financial oversight or bears the costs of banking failures. Paraguay’s legacies of political patronage make it necessary to examine political and corporate connections and changes to public-fund investment rules. The social toll and the Colorado question Paraguay has been here before. Between 1995 and 1998, 13 banks and 35 financial firms closed, with direct costs estimated by the IMF at 10% to 13% of the country’s GDP. This preceded a smaller bank crisis in the early 2000s. Both ordeals exposed weak supervision and connected lending. Paraguay’s deposit guarantee, which covers balances up to about $38,000, is meant to limit depositor losses, and the Paraguayan Central Bank insists that failure is isolated in the latest case. Yet account transfers have already strained the system, producing outages at several banking institutions. Yet for most Paraguayans, the crisis was experienced not through technical financial or macroeconomic indicators but at the stark level of seeing from their phones that they couldn’t access their money. Wages, pensions and savings froze simultaneously. Young Ueno employees burned their company cards outside the Labor Ministry, demanding unpaid wages. Riot police used pepper spray and rubber bullets against depositors marching on Congress. For small businesses that banked and paid staff through Ueno, the real economy stopped. This widespread anger challenges the ruling party’s claims to the economic vision they cite as the engine for future growth. Whether it leads to institutional change or a reshuffle within the Colorado Party remains an open question. The test is how Paraguayan legislators and regulators will move forward and whether they separate banking supervision and public deposits from partisan and business networks. In any case, the myth of the “Dubai of South America” has come under serious scrutiny. While the protests were noteworthy, the Colorado Party has for now managed to resolve its own internal crisis by quickly sacrificing key political elites, including the president. Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty ImagesNearly every country in the world has acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem. It’s hard to ignore, as billions of people suffer through increasingly destructive storms and extreme heat. In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are driving global temperatures higher. Yet those emissions are still hitting record levels, and global negotiations over how to slow climate change routinely end with weak promises. There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader. As a professor of environmental studies and international relations at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade. My research lab investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks. As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress. Here are five tactics among many that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change: 1. Say we can’t afford it “We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations. At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding. They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target. Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused. The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030. In reality, affordability is really about priorities. For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy. Military budgets tell a similar story. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons. Recent research points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels. The money exists. The question is where governments choose to spend it. 2. Promise to fix it later Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so drastic emissions cuts can wait or even be avoided. This technological optimism has deep roots. In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “stabilization wedge” approach to addressing climate change. It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide. Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy. Carbon capture and storage allows fossil fuel operations to continue by pumping their emissions underground. Congressional Budget Office Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue. Scientists, including one of the original authors, have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve. Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back to the fossil fuel giant BP. Yet the same logic is now present in agreements emerging from recent climate talks. 3. Water down the promise Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding. At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels. It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement. However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead. Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most. U.S. Climate Envoy John Kerry and other delegates huddle for final negotiating at the closing sessions of COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021. Kiara Worth/UNFCCC, CC BY-NC-SA The first fossil fuel language in a U.N. climate pact came out diluted. Four years later, at COP30, 88 countries backed a roadmap to move the world away from using fossil fuels, but the final decision left it out. 4. Make promises, then fail to deliver Countries are really good at making pledges to help, but not so much at providing the funding. In 2009, wealthy countries promised developing countries $100 billion annually to help them address climate risks. They missed that target for over a decade. Even when they did claim to hit the target, they relied largely on dubious accounting, with donors counting fossil fuel projects, airports and even ice cream shops as climate aid. The Loss and Damage Fund created at COP27 in 2021 to help countries manage disaster damage shows a similar pattern. Only about half of the roughly $822 million pledged had been paid in five years later, and the fund has not paid out a single dollar to a country hit by a disaster. Nepal has emerged as a critical test of the fund’s integrity. After a glacier collapse triggered a sudden flood that killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal in August 2026, the government estimated the country had suffered $2.7 billion in damage. Nepal requested $20 million, and, in a first, the fund’s board agreed in October to “provisionally set aside” $21.6 million, but that’s only the beginning of the paperwork. 5. Make decisions without everyone at the table Decisions at the U.N. climate conference are taken by consensus, meaning they’re considered adopted when no country formally objects. This act is marked by the banging of a gavel. At COP28 in Dubai, the conference president “gaveled through” a key decision before representatives of the Alliance of Small Island States had reached the room, meaning they had no chance to object. The lead negotiator for the islands’ group told the meeting that they would have objected, as they considered it too weak to keep warming to the agreed limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) within reach. In 2025, at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, a similar scene played out. After swiftly gaveling through many decisions, the conference president failed to recognize Colombia’s request to speak until after the gavel had fallen. Colombia objected that the text of the formal decision failed to discuss a transition away from fossil fuels. The COP president later apologized but said the decision could not be reopened. What to watch for at COP31 At COP31, my team and I will be watching for decisions about financial support, whether talk of technology crowds out reducing fossil fuel use, and who gets a voice. Much of what matters at these conferences happens out of the spotlight. Plenary sessions, where decisions are formally adopted, are the part most people see. But the wording of those decisions is usually worked out in smaller rooms and closed-door huddles among a handful of delegations. Small delegations can’t staff every room, and some rooms are closed to observers. My team will be tracking what happens, whose proposals survive, and what quietly drops out between drafts of the agreement text. We’ll also be paying attention to who, quietly or not, says “no.” Ridwan Intisaar Mahbub, a graduate student in public diplomacy, and Richie Sanchez, an undergraduate student in environmental studies at USC, contributed research for this article. Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty ImagesData centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections. A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development. The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers. According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%. Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits. I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns. Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms. Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity. AP Photo/Mike Stewart Disrupting political polarization In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines. Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points. The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally. Allies and adversaries Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations. These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away. The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests. William Lawrence, a Democrat who flipped a red House seat in Michigan in the 2026 midterm elections, speaks on the campaign trail. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change. Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements. Politics as usual As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president. It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built. What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day. As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring. ee2e69986711e4f8: PETALING JAYA: Pejuang information chief Rafique Rashid Ali has defended Attorney-General Dusuki Mokhtar over alleged mistakes in a court order concerning Najib Razak's house arrest, saying the AG should not be blamed for a document prepared by the court.
Rafique, a lawyer by profession, said those questioning the errors should ask the Kuala Lumpur High Court for an explanation, rather than point fingers at Dusuki or the lawyers involved in the case.
The controversy centres on a court order issued after Najib paid a RM50 million fine on Nov 6.

The document purportedly called for his immediate release but also said he was to serve the remainder of his prison sentence in the SRC International case under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, following the payment of his RM50 million fine.
Rafique said there appeared to be confusion over who was responsible for preparing such documents.
“In criminal cases, neither the defence lawyers nor the AG are involved. The court prepares the documents,” he said in a statement.
He said court officials were responsible for preparing documents involving the detention or release of prisoners, payment of fines and return of passports.
He said the High Court's criminal registry, which handles paperwork for criminal cases, should therefore explain the mistakes in the order.
Rafique said this was different from civil cases, where lawyers for the winning party usually prepare the court order and send it to the opposing side for approval before submitting it to the court.
He also criticised lawyers and former government legal officers who had questioned the wording of Najib's order, saying some appeared unfamiliar with how criminal courts worked.
“I respect your views, but there must be an understanding of court procedures before commenting,” he said.
Earlier today, Dusuki described the errors in the order as obvious, saying they should have been spotted if the document had been properly checked.

The Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) has since sought to delay Najib's transfer to house arrest while questions are resolved over his SRC prison sentence and how it affects the separate 15-year jail term he received in the 1MDB case.
Rafique previously criticised the AGC's handling of Najib's case, questioning why it waited until Najib had paid the fine before raising concerns over how his house arrest should be carried out.

4b382a44aa6e09e6: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails.
The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures.
Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information.

The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails.

The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required.

Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed.
Although some customers insist their DMARC, SPF, and DKIM settings are compliant, many more have reported that once they set them to Microsoft's preferences, email began flowing once more.

SPF must pass for the sending domain (the domain's DNS record should accurately list authorized IP addresses/hosts). DKIM must pass to validate email integrity and authenticity. DMARC must have at least p=none and align with either SPF or DKIM (preferably both).
The Register asked the Windows giant for more information, but we have yet to receive a response.

To make matters worse, the glitch also appears to be intermittent. A resend attempt might succeed following a rejection. To compound the situation, the rejection error message may also be vague about what caused the bounce in the first place.
A moderator in Microsoft's support forum acknowledged the bug and said it was "classified as a service degradation."

"Microsoft is actively investigating the underlying cause of this email delivery issue, and engineering teams are actively analyzing service telemetry and customer-provided data to identify the source of the issue."

Still. It could be worse. Earlier today, several users in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa were affected by another Microsoft whoopsie – a "recent service change" that caused some connections to be abruptly terminated. Outlook on the web, as well as the Purview and Defender portals were all affected.
Microsoft reverted the change in the Exchange Online front-end infrastructure, and all was well.
It has yet to say what else, if anything, might have changed in its email services to cause legitimate messages to bounce back. ®

Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made

—By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm

This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story.
Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests

Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction.
The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree.

For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.
Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate.

c9312c495ec193c1: MELAKA: Kementerian Dalam Negeri mengambil sikap berhati-hati dalam tindakan meletakkan bekas perdana menteri, Najib Razak, bawah tahanan rumah tanpa menyelesaikan tafsiran bercanggah berhubung perintah pelepasan mahkamah, yang boleh dianggap sebagai penahanan salah.

Menteri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, berkata pihaknya berada dalam dilema antara pengampunan bersyarat diberikan kepada Najib — yang membenarkannya menjalani baki hukuman penjara kes SRC International bawah tahanan rumah selepas menjelaskan denda RM50 juta — dan satu perintah mahkamah menggunakan istilah 'dilepaskan'.
"Tahanan rumah lain, pelepasan lain. Jadi, kalau letak pada kedudukan kami, kami hendak pakai mana satu? Sebab ini dokumen undang-undang, ini istilah undang-undang.
"Negara kita ada undang-undang, dan kalau ada kekeliruan, kita rujuk mahkamahlah," katanya,” katanya kepada pemberita selepas bertemu dengan komuniti nelayan di Pengkalan Kling.

Saifuddin berkata, pelepasan sepenuhnya bermakna Jabatan Penjara tidak lagi mempunyai kuasa ke atas Najib, manakala tahanan rumah pula memerlukan jabatan itu kekal memegang hak kawalan terhadap beliau.
Beliau berkata, pihaknya telah menerima surat daripada urus setia lembaga pengampunan dan menghormati keputusan tersebut.
"Berkaitan titah Yang di-Pertuan Agong, itu tidak ada siapa usik," katanya, sambil menambah kementerian telah memohon nasihat peguam negara disebabkan wujudnya tafsiran undang-undang berbeza.
Beliau berkata, mahkamah merupakan saluran wajar menyelesaikan isu tersebut, sambil menyatakan pihaknya akan menghormati apa jua keputusan diputuskan.

Ditanya bilakah peguam negara akan merujuk perkara tersebut ke mahkamah, Saifuddin berkata, beliau tidak mempunyai maklumat mengenai bila prosiding akan dimulakan atau pihak mana yang akan membawa isu berkenaan ke mahkamah.
Pada 6 Nov, Umno umum telah menjelaskan denda RM50 juta bagi pihak Najib, sekali gus membolehkan beliau menjalani baki hukuman penjaranya bawah tahanan rumah.
Namun, Jabatan Peguam Negara (AGC) menyeru pelaksanaannya ditangguhkan sementara menunggu penjelasan berhubung frasa bercanggah dalam perintah mahkamah berkenaan.
