4a92101b327c948a: MELAKA, Nov 9 — Competitively paid job opportunities and assistance for the upkeep of places of worship are among the key issues raised by the Indian community in the Paya Rumput state constituency, which they hope will receive attention from the candidates elected during the Melaka state election.

Mechanical engineer Sathesh Kumaar A/L Gunasegaran, 24, said graduate employability and competitive salaries were important benchmarks in determining who should be elected to serve the residents of Paya Rumput.

He said the state government and the incoming elected representative should formulate initiatives to narrow the salary gap in Melaka and bring it closer to the level offered in states such as Johor, in order to prevent the migration of local talent.

“Among the issues I can highlight for the younger generation is, first and foremost, the unemployment rate. Perhaps Melaka is not on par with states such as Johor in terms of how they have brought about changes in salaries and job opportunities.
“Besides that, I also hope candidates can introduce activities or programmes that benefit school students and help improve their education and living standards,” he told Bernama.

K Selvie a/p Kannon, 58, said the Indian community in the constituency appreciated federal government assistance such as the Rahmah Cash Contribution (STR), Rahmah Basic Contribution (SARA) and other forms of aid, but also hoped that the needs of places of worship would be addressed. — Bernama pic

Sharing similar views, electrical and electronic engineering graduate Kuhan, 24, who goes by a single name, said Gen Z youths like him faced difficulties entering the job market if existing industrial areas in Paya Rumput were not fully utilised.

“It’s really not easy to find a job. Even as a fresh graduate, I’m actually struggling to get one. But honestly, I feel that if we vote for the right party that can establish a proper foundation for our country, we as Gen Z can lead the country and have a better future with a stronger foundation,” he said.

Apart from employment and salary issues, the Indian community in Paya Rumput also hopes that the welfare of its religious institutions, particularly places of worship, will receive attention from the constituency’s incoming elected representative.

Sharing similar views, electrical and electronic engineering graduate Kuhan, 24, said Gen Z youths like him faced difficulties entering the job market if existing industrial areas in Paya Rumput were not fully utilised. — Bernama pic

K Selvie a/p Kannon, 58, said the Indian community in the constituency appreciated federal government assistance such as the Rahmah Cash Contribution (STR), Rahmah Basic Contribution (SARA) and other forms of aid, but also hoped that the needs of places of worship would be addressed.
The mother of five hopes that the elected representative for Paya Rumput will help ease the financial burden of relocating a temple from its former site to a new site purchased by the community.
“This assistance is not for personal gain, but for the benefit of the younger generation and our grandchildren and future generations, so that they can worship in comfort and safety,” she said.

7a2813cd7ac89274: MELAKA, Nov 9 — Deepavali celebrations by the Melaka Chetti community at Kampung Chetti here on Sunday had a distinctively festive atmosphere, with the Festival of Lights marked by a spirit of goodwill, harmony and family togetherness.

Although only about 30 families are understood to remain in the heritage village, the lively Deepavali celebrations, featuring several unique traditions, demonstrate the minority community’s continued commitment to preserving its distinctive customs and identity, passed down since the era of the Melaka Sultanate.

Deepavali celebrations in this heritage settlement differ from those observed by other Hindu communities, particularly among Indians. Among the distinctive traditions is the practice of temple priests delivering prasadam and visiting homes to bless each family.

However, public understanding and knowledge of the unique culture and history of the Melaka Chetti community remain limited, particularly among those outside the community, leading to misconceptions about its true identity.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Preparations for an array of festive delicacies add to the excitement of Deepavali as Wenila Nadarajan (left), a member of the Chetti (Indian Peranakan) community, joins her child and a friend in preparing a variety of dishes to serve guests visiting her home in Kampung Chetti, Kota Laksamana, November 8, 2026. — Bernama pic

Fortunately, there are still members of this community who understand and remain committed to preserving their identity, including Wenila Nadarajan, 46, to ensure the community’s continued existence in the country, particularly in Melaka.

Wenila, who runs a Chetti food business in Jalan Tengkera, described herself as often playing the role of a storyteller to answer questions from the public about the origins of the Indian Peranakan community, which practises Hinduism but speaks a form of Malay creole.

“At my shop, I am like a storyteller. Whenever people come, I have to explain who the Chetti people are because they do not know. Many people, especially those from outside Melaka, are unfamiliar with the community.

“Many assume that the Chetti community is Muslim because they speak Malay, or because they do not know how to speak Tamil, although that is not the case for everyone. In the past, the Chetti community spoke Baba Malay, but nowadays many also marry Indians and Chinese, so the language has become a mixture,” she told Bernama at her home here.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The aroma of traditional dishes and variety of delicacies add to the festive atmosphere of the Deepavali celebration with the Chetti (Indian Peranakan) community at Kampung Chetti, Kota Laksamana. Dishes such as lontong, mutton curry, ‘roti jala’ and ‘tosai’ not only whet the appetites of guests but also showcase the unique culinary heritage of the Chetti community, which blends Indian and Malay influences, making the Festival of Lights celebration even more special in an atmosphere of warmth and goodwill. — Bernama pic

Wenila also hopes that efforts to promote and raise awareness of the Chetti Melaka community, including through school history textbooks, can be expanded so that younger generations become more familiar with its existence.
However, beneath the pride in the community’s distinctive identity and traditions lies deep concern over the future of the heritage village, which is increasingly threatened by rapid development.
A native of the village, Shanmugam Raja, 57, said the historic settlement must be protected from physical development that could wipe out the community’s culture.

“This place should be preserved. If the village is not gazetted and uncontrolled development is allowed, it will affect the settlement. If the village disappears, the Chetti community, along with our culture and heritage, will quickly become extinct and be lost.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Chetti (Indian Peranakan) resident R. Shanmugam speaks to members of the media about the Deepavali celebration with the Chetti community at his home in Kampung Chetti, Kota Laksamana, November 8, 2026. — Bernama pic

“One thing I have observed is that when members of a community do not live together in one area, practising their culture and traditions is not difficult, but there is a lack of encouragement. Here, all the neighbours practise them together, making it easier and more enjoyable,” he said.

The information technology professional also expressed concern about younger generations who move away and later return to the village with the mindset of being ‘guests’ rather than ‘hosts’, consequently reducing their sense of responsibility towards carrying on their customs and traditions.

“I have noticed that many among the younger generation, when they return, do not see themselves as hosts but as guests. When this happens, they do not take part in the activities here. That is the problem, and over time, these cultural practices will disappear,” he said. — Bernama
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A lively and heartwarming atmosphere marks the Deepavali celebration at Kampung Chetti, Kota Laksamana, November 8, 2026, as members of the Baba and Nyonya (Chinese Peranakan) community join the Chetti (Indian Peranakan) community in celebrating the Festival of Lights in a spirit of joy and togetherness. — Bernama pic
ed3c13dab30b183f: JASIN, Nov 9 — As campaigning for the 16th Melaka State Election intensifies, a kelong (offshore fishing platform) off Pantai Siring here offers visitors a peaceful retreat, allowing them to unwind and experience the quieter side of coastal life.
Just a five-minute boat ride from shore, Kelong Tiga Nur, run by a local fisherman, attracts anglers and leisure seekers looking to relax while enjoying scenic views of nearby islands.

Its operator, Raduan Bodot, 62, said the kelong, which began operations in early January last year, has attracted visitors from other states and Singapore, with some returning regularly to enjoy its relaxing atmosphere and facilities.
“We get bookings almost every day from visitors wanting to spend the night at the kelong. Some have even booked their fishing trips as far ahead as September next year.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Fisherman Raduan Bodot, 62, showing his octopus catch, which is used as bait by anglers, during a survey off Pantai Siring. — Bernama pic

“I always put our visitors’ comfort first. That’s why we provide bedrooms, mattresses, a kitchen, a surau (prayer room) and bathrooms, as well as breakfast, so they can enjoy their stay here,” he told Bernama here recently.
According to Raduan, the kelong can accommodate up to 20 people at a time, with a daily rental fee of RM1,200.
He said the idea of building the kelong came about as he looked for ways to earn extra income amid declining fish catches and the challenges of making a living as a fisherman.
“At my age, I can’t go out to sea as often as I used to, and with fish catches getting smaller, it’s becoming even harder.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Some of the seashells used to catch octopuses during a survey off Pantai Siring. — Bernama pic
“So, I started thinking about what I could do to overcome the problem and eventually decided to build a kelong,” he said, adding that he named it after his three children.

Measuring about 50 feet by 100 feet, the kelong was built entirely using Raduan’s savings, accumulated through careful spending, with construction beginning in December last year before it opened in January this year.
Raduan also supplements his income by selling octopuses to visitors who use them as bait when fishing around the kelong.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Fisherman Raduan Bodot, 62, looking at his octopus catch, which is used as bait by anglers, during a survey off Pantai Siring. — Bernama pic
He said he started catching octopuses two to three years ago after noticing demand for them among anglers.
Interestingly, Raduan places seashells on the seabed to provide shelter for octopuses, making them easier to catch.
He said smaller octopuses sell for RM5 each, while larger ones fetch RM10, helping him earn extra income.
Raduan also hoped to secure funding from government agencies to upgrade the kelong’s facilities and help boost tourism in the Pantai Siring area. — Bernama
1c18af50ff5def54: FLORIDA (Uruguay), Nov 9 — Pope Leo XIV told men to treat their wives with respect yesterday, as he concluded the first leg of his tour of Latin America, which is plagued by gender-based violence.

“Dear fathers and grandfathers... treat your wives with respect, ask for forgiveness and live with integrity, even when doing so requires sacrifice,” the head of the Catholic Church said during a homily in Uruguay.
Over 3,800 women were killed in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2024 because of their gender, according to the UN’s regional economic mission.
Over the last five years, the region has recorded nearly 20,000 femicides, most of them committed by the victim’s current or former partner.
Leo is on a 12-day tour of the continent where he served as a missionary and a bishop before becoming pope.
He wrapped up the first leg of his visit in largely secular Uruguay with an open-air mass outside a basilica in the south-central city of Florida.

This handout picture released by the Vatican Media shows Pope Leo XIV delivering a speech during a ceremony at the Libertad Palace in Buenos Aires on November 8, 2026. — Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media/AFP pic
The basilica is home to a shrine linked to Uruguay’s fight for independence from Spanish colonial rule.
Thousands of worshippers packed the city’s main square for the service, basking in warm sunshine after several days of unusually cold weather triggered by an exceptionally strong El Nino.
“I think it’s very important that the Pope came because it strengthens the Church’s presence in our country,” 22-year-old Ivanna Fisichella, who attended the mass, told AFP.
Evangelina Campero, 57, highlighted “the effort the pope is making” by embarking on a gruelling tour just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.
“The message is to give it your all,” she said.

The 71-year-old pontiff will later travel to Argentina, where he will meet President Javier Milei, a right-wing libertarian whose austerity policies have drawn sharp criticism from the Catholic Church.
The high point of his visit is expected to be the third and final leg of his tour, which takes him to Peru.
Leo has a special connection to the Andean country where he spent nearly two decades as a missionary, including eight years as a bishop. — AFP

ee24aec4fc806a1b: Someone left your organisation in the spring. Can they still open the project share? Most infrastructure leads would want to check before answering, and that pause is the subject of a dinner The Register and LucidLink are hosting for senior technology, infrastructure, and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair.

The trouble is the copies. A busy folder lives on the file server, in a sync client, on a couple of laptops and in the share set up for an agency last year, and each copy carries its own permissions. Locking down one leaves the others as they were. Then there's the tool a team built for itself because the approved one was too slow, which IT may not know exists.

The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, and that's what makes it worth going. People say what actually happened in their own shop and how they caught it. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers round the table. Nobody presents.

The talk moves on to unstructured data that keeps growing, the duplicate storage that comes with it, and how to get access back under control without throwing out the storage and governance you've already paid for.
Drinks are at 6.30pm and dinner around one table runs until 9pm. Places are limited.

05bd9f0351a0c3a2: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”

Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.

“Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.

These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.

Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.”

ce8b9f01db91226b: Japanese electronics giant Iris Ohyama has taken down its online store after discovering that attackers may have accessed the personal information of 7.7 million customers, leaving shoppers unable to place orders.

The retailer, which sells everything from home appliances and furniture to pet supplies, first disclosed the incident on October 29, a day after discovering a suspicious file on a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza ecommerce operation.
Iris Plaza immediately suspended its website and associated systems and began investigating, subsequently confirming unauthorized access.

Iris Ohyama has since revealed that the potentially compromised cloud environment contained personal information belonging to approximately 5.8 million registered customers, including former members, and another 1.9 million people who had purchased products without creating an account or participated in promotional campaigns.

The potentially exposed information includes names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, gender, and passwords, although the company says the exact information at risk varies between customers.

Some of that data, including passwords, was encrypted, but Iris Ohyama hasn't explained what protection was used. It has advised customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords elsewhere to change them, presumably before someone else gets the opportunity.

There is some good news for anyone who has handed over their credit card details, as the retailer says it didn't store payment information in the affected cloud service and that it hasn't been compromised.

It remains unclear whether the attackers actually made off with any personal information. In its FAQ, Iris Plaza says it is still investigating the possibility of a data leak and has yet to establish the full extent of the intrusion.

Meanwhile, Iris Plaza's website is still down, and the company isn't saying when it'll be back. Orders are also taking longer to ship, while customers trying to cancel a purchase have been told they may have to turn the delivery driver away if their parcel arrives before the cancellation is processed.

Fortunately for anyone desperate to buy a new rice cooker, Iris Plaza's stores on Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, and auPAY Market are still operating. The company says it has found no evidence that those stores were affected.

Iris Ohyama has reported the incident to Japanese authorities and says it will contact potentially affected customers individually. It has also warned shoppers to watch out for phishing emails, fraudulent calls, and fake websites impersonating the retailer.
The company has yet to identify the cloud provider involved, explain how the attackers got in, or establish whether any of those 7.7 million records actually left its systems. ®

9db69e673cf8917a: LONDON, Nov 9 — Once homeless and destitute, Brighton have defied the odds to emerge as the most unexpected Premier League title contenders since Leicester’s fairytale run a decade ago.
Brighton head into the international break proudly sitting second in the Premier League after yesterday’s 2-0 win against Brentford.
Fabian Hurzeler’s side have moved above far wealthier clubs including Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea, with leaders Arsenal only five points ahead of the high-flying Seagulls.
Brighton’s climb towards the top of the table could easily be written off as a brief blip before the league’s traditional powers reassert their supremacy.

But that would be to ignore the rock-solid foundations laid by Hurzeler and Albion’s astute owner Tony Bloom, a professional gambler who has transformed Brighton since taking a major gamble when he bought the club in 2009.
Brighton have won seven of their 10 league games this season, a blistering run that included a pair of statement victories.
Swatting aside champions Arsenal 3-0 in September while wearing a commemorative kit to mark the club’s 125th anniversary was a memorable afternoon.

But beating City 1-0 in Manchester in October — just days after losing a League Cup penalty shoot-out at the Etihad Stadium — showed Brighton have the bloody-minded streak required to cope with the pitfalls of a title race.

In a season in which City are distracted by their appeal against a guilty verdict for financial breaches, Liverpool and Chelsea are rebuilding under new managers and Manchester United are in disarray, there could be an opening for Brighton to replicate Leicester’s fairytale title triumph in 2016.
Catching Arsenal will not be easy but Hurzeler admitted there is mounting excitement around his club.
Asked when supporters could start to dream of a title bid, Hurzeler said: “They should be always excited if they watch our game, and that’s our job to make them excited.
“I always say they can dream, they can have high expectations on us, but these are things we can’t control.”
Hurzeler became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when Bloom lured him from St Pauli in 2024.
Born in Texas, the 33-year-old German had a modest playing career before turning to coaching, where he caught Bloom’s eye by leading St Pauli into the Bundesliga.
His work at Brighton has been even more impressive, taking them to a pair of eighth place finishes in the Premier League and into this season’s Uefa Conference League.
Stampeding bull
Bloom has also been a gleeful disruptor of football’s establishment.
When lifelong fan Bloom purchased Brighton, they were languishing in the third tier with significant debts and playing at a ramshackle athletics stadium on the outskirts of the town.
Implementing the ground-breaking use of analytics and advanced scouting technology, Bloom has helped Brighton sign unknown youngsters and turn them into top-level stars.
He brought Brighton back to a purpose-built new stadium in 2011, sparking a golden era that serves as a stark contrast to their chaotic past.
“Anyone walking into Brighton today compared to even 15 years ago would not think it was the same football club,” sporting director Mike Cave said.
In keeping with the hipster seaside town’s colourful community, Brighton has always been one of English football’s more eccentric outposts since their foundation in 1901.
Trophies might have been in short supply on the South coast, but Brighton have a habit of giving their fans unforgettable moments — for better or worse.
A 1983 FA Cup final appearance against Manchester United featured a famous miss by Gordon Smith that could have secured the club’s first major silverware.
Brighton were thrashed by United in the replay and crashed out of the top-flight the same season.

An even more catastrophic relegation from the Football League in 1997 was only avoided on the last day of the season after a live bull — used as Hereford’s mascot — stampeded onto the pitch during a dramatic draw that saved Brighton from potential oblivion.
The club spent two years in exile, playing their matches 70 miles from Brighton at Gillingham, after the Goldstone Ground, their home since 1902, was sold because of escalating debts.
From the depths of despair, Brighton have emerged unscathed.
“What got this football club through was the determination of its fans. The bucket collections. The protests. The refusal to accept the Albion should disappear,” Bloom said. — AFP

You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube. Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live.

The Democratic party has seized control of Congress and state governments around the country. It's easy to see this entirely as a rebuke of Trump and his policies, but blowback against AI, datacenters, and the tech industry played a role too, if the past week of chaos in markets and Silicon Valley is any indication.

Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, El Reg Editor In Chief Matt Rosoff, and special guest, senior reporter at The Verge, Elizabeth Lopatto, to talk about what the winds of political change mean for the tech industry.

Now it's easy to see this as a blowback against Trump and Republican politics. There's a lot of indication that the tech industry was kind of on the ballot this year, too.

After all, they cozied up hard to Trump in his first two years in office in a bid to push AI and promote datacenter projects, and people have been none too happy about any of that. Thank you. It's lovely to be here.

d8283c68ecae5ae4: "AI delusion" remains loosely defined, but most of us know it when we see it: exaggerated faith in the technology's power, applicability, or nature, coupled with a refusal to acknowledge its limitations.

It's bad in the individual, as when an elderly relative emails you a hallucination-laden ChatGPT summary. It's worse in management, when your boss insists that AI slop is genius marketing content at a bargain rate. It is terrifying in tech CEOs. It is not, thankfully, compulsory.

Consider three recent examples of technology leadership in the age of AI. One would be Pythonesque were the disconnect with engineers and the public not so profound. Another risks becoming a business-school case study in how to demolish customer trust. The third offers something less fashionable: robust pragmatism. Saving the best till last, y'all.

Case 1: we present for your consideration Sam Altman of OpenAI, one of the few actually at the controls of the singularity machine. It seems churlish to pluck just one luscious fruit out of that cornucopia of choices, yet we must. Sam Altman thinks it is a sin against the natural order that so much RAM is idling in machines owned by individuals, organizations, and anywhere that isn't Big AI. It's oh so inefficient. How convenient that the efficient allocation of scarce resources should favor the business he runs. Free market schmarket.
Altman has since said his remarks were taken out of context and that he wants consumers to have as much memory as they like. The efficiency argument still reveals whose priorities come first.

This is the best kind of delusion, one with an undeniable truth at its core – memory does indeed get used far more intensively in AI model makers and inference servers than in your laptop. For a business selling the future, treating privately owned hardware as an inefficient allocation of resources has a distinctly Soviet flavor, and the American right has vowed to stamp out socialist extremism. Get on with it, chaps, you've only got two years left. That Altman can't see this is the best bit of the misconception.

There are two potential root causes of this Marxist-Leninist-Altmanism. One is that he's mathed the math and worked out that the only way OpenAI can hit the numbers is if it gets every last byte in the world, hot off the fab. The other is that you can't run on-prem on an 8 GB state-mandated Chromebook, and on-prem is otherwise going to twist his melon until it falls off.

Case 2: Andy Yen, CEO of Proton, the company behind Proton Mail and Proton VPN. You, me, and the household cat know ProtonMail as the secondary email that's worth paying for. You want the best recovery backup email for Gmail, you want it as an accessible end-to-end encrypted email service. You want it because it is all about stable spotless security, all about the end users, all about being there when you absolutely need it. It is safe to recommend, and you do.

Or rather that's what you thought about ProtonMail et al until the same day you learned about Andy Yen's alleged behavior. Leaked comms reported by 404 Media allege Yen saw Proton as a company that must make its numbers come what may, and one path to do that was to AI-code at maximum velocity.

Engineers who wanted to test the results for security were losers – fax machine operators in the internet age – and he didn't want them, or so the report claimed. No more engineers, just product managers in a Claude terminal. He allegedly imparted this vision through aggression, belittling employees in front of their peers, and swinging his big ol' reinterview job chopper.

More generally, running a toxic workplace should lead to instant dismissal and loss of license to be in charge of anything more sentient than a sausage machine. That AI is involved is not AI's fault. Misunderstanding the brand and the customer base so, so badly – that's the delusion.
ProtonMail has a unique niche, an important part of the whole. People depend on it because privacy and security are the proposition.

Putting velocity of coding above that is arrant stupidity. Nobody cares. Unless new features and products increase security, they'll only matter outside the niche, where one might argue that Proton products cannot compete. Not knowing that, has the potential to destroy a brand overnight. Yen wouldn't be the first CEO to cause a company some trouble by revealing what they really think, but this one matters. Things are being rowed back – no more reinterviewing to prove allegiance to AI at all costs, and an employee has said it's not quite as bad as all that.

Case 3: Linus Torvalds. He reports that AI-based kernel code has not saturated the production pipeline, is useful when treated properly, and the kernel cadence is expanding following a stabilization period. The high-pressure AI patch spigot turned on; the appropriate plumbing was created to regulate and filter; and he is much happier now.

It's a nuanced story, and nuance is so often a dirty word in the industry. Torvalds' happiness is not a guarantee that everything in the garden is in fact lovely, but the Linus vibe is as good as any – and it's better than most predictive metrics. He is hitting his numbers, which are the quality of the code and the speed at which changes match what users need in a changing world. The numbers do not involve margins, profits, shareholder value, or driving massive investment before the gig's up.

Put another way, Torvalds has managed the arrival of AI to probably the most important codebase ever, and he has done it with, not in spite of, the most diverse and independently minded dev team that ever came through the merge window, and it's barely news. If only they gave Oscars for this sort of thing.

There is no better advert for sanity, nor for FOSS's unique and infinitely valuable ability to remain responsive to market forces without market dependency. Freedom cures delusion. Even AI delusion. It's a helluva drug. ®

Millions celebrate the annual festival of lights with fireworks in one of the world’s most polluted capitals, worsening winter smog fuelled by vehicle emissions, farm fires and industry.

Vehicles account for 23 per cent of Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20 per cent, according to India’s environment ministry.
Industry, including coal-fired power plants, contributes about nine per cent.
The largest share, 27 per cent, comes from secondary particles, formed when gases released by vehicles, industry, power plants and biomass burning react in the atmosphere.

"The attackers' access within TUMonline was largely logged," said Dr Alexander Braun, CIO at TUM, in the disclosure. "After analyzing these logs, we currently assume that no other data from TUMonline was compromised, such as grades or college applications. We are continuing to investigate this."

TUM is directing users to reset their passwords through Microsoft 365 where possible. Those without MFA already configured must instead use a German electronic ID or request a reset email while connected to the campus network.
The university also warned users to watch for phishing and fraud, and to change any passwords reused elsewhere.

TUM ranks first in Germany and 25th worldwide in the QS university rankings. The STEM-focused institution reports 51,954 students across its German campuses and TUM Asia in Singapore, plus 12,850 employees. ®
a9830ddebfcc4a96: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 9 — The Ministry of Health (MOH) has prepared 85 Emergency Medical Teams comprising 387 personnel to respond to possible flooding during the 2026/2027 North-east Monsoon (MTL).

In a statement today, the ministry said these comprised 36 Rapid Assessment and Health Rapid Response Teams, 34 Medical Rapid Response Teams and 15 Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) teams.

“The teams will be mobilised as required to conduct health risk assessments, provide medical services and emergency treatment, carry out surveillance and control of infectious diseases, as well as provide mental health and psychosocial support to flood victims,” it said.

The ministry has also made available 128 vehicles to support personnel mobilisation and field operations, while flood-related medicine supplies at warehouses operated by concessionaire suppliers remain stable, with stocks estimated to last between one and three months.

Through the National Crisis Preparedness and Response Centre (CPRC), State Health Departments, District Health Offices and healthcare facilities nationwide, the ministry has also stepped up preparedness to ensure continued healthcare services, particularly in flood-prone areas.

The National CPRC has been in Alert Mode since October 27, with continuous monitoring of flood situations, healthcare facility preparedness and coordination of response measures with State Health Departments and relevant agencies.

The ministry said healthcare facilities at risk of flooding had also been identified, together with alternative facilities in the event of operational disruptions. Plans were also in place for the early transfer of high-risk patients, including pregnant women and those requiring haemodialysis.

The ministry said the risk of flooding could increase if prolonged rain coincided with high tides.

At relief centres, the ministry provides health assessments, infectious disease monitoring, environmental hygiene inspections, food and water safety checks, vector control, as well as mental health and psychosocial support.
These measures are aimed at reducing the risk of flood-related illnesses, including diarrhoea, food poisoning, leptospirosis and respiratory tract infections.
The ministry also advised the public to use clean and safe drinking water, consume properly cooked food and avoid food contaminated by floodwaters.
People were also advised to maintain personal and environmental hygiene, wash their hands frequently with clean water and soap, and avoid direct contact with potentially contaminated floodwaters.

ab138347ee884e3e: NEW YORK, Nov 9 — Chips made by US chip titan Nvidia push the boundaries of artificial intelligence, but its leader Jensen Huang is in the spotlight over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Unknown to the public just four years ago, the 63-year-old is a powerful entrepreneur, drawing stadium crowds as he presents cutting-edge components essential to the development of AI tools like ChatGPT.
Media reports last week said US intelligence officials believe Huang grew close to a Chinese executive who was funnelling information to Beijing.
Nvidia’s board said yesterday it had opened a probe into the CEO and co-founder, who acknowledged having been unfaithful to his wife and said he was “deeply sorry.”

Big tech’s insatiable appetite for chips designed by Nvidia, known as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), has catapulted the California chipmaker to a market valuation of US$4.5 trillion (RM18.2 trillion), among the world’s largest.

Its meteoric rise has made Huang one of the world’s richest people — worth around US$160 billion, according to Forbes — thanks to the roughly four per cent stake he holds in the company he founded three decades ago with two friends in a Silicon Valley diner.
He has become a close informal adviser on AI to Donald Trump, travelling with the US president on Air Force One on a trip to Beijing earlier this year.
That is an area of concern to US officials who believe he has been involved with the alleged spy, Alice Huang, who is linked to a Singapore-based data centre company, according to the New York Times.
Despite their shared surname, the pair are not related.
Early life
Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang — originally named Jen-Hsun — embodies the American success story.
At nine years old, he was sent away with his brother to boarding school in small-town Kentucky.
His uncle recommended the school to his Taiwanese parents believing it to be a prestigious institution, though it was actually a school for troubled youth.

Too young to be a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers. With his poor English, he was bullied and forced to clean toilets — a two-year ordeal that transformed him.
“We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough,” he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.
But “the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there,” Huang said.
Brought home by his parents who had by then settled in the north-western US state of Oregon, he graduated from university at just 20 and joined AMD, then LSI Logic, to design chips — his passion.

But he wanted to go further and founded Nvidia in 1993 to “solve problems that normal computers can’t,” using semiconductors powerful enough to handle 3D graphics, he said during an interview on the “No Priors” podcast.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang waves after a welcome ceremony for US President Donald Trump at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing May 14, 2026. Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade. — AFP pic
‘As fast as we can’
Nvidia created the first GPU in 1999, riding the intersection of video games, data centres, cloud computing and now generative AI.
Always dressed in a black T-shirt and leather jacket, Huang sports a Nvidia logo tattoo and has a taste for sports cars.
One former high-ranking Nvidia employee described him to AFP as “the most driven person” he’d ever met.
He has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade.
“That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention,” but “it’s not grounded on facts,” he told CBS News in September.
“We should go as fast as we can” on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.
Street food
On visits to his native Taiwan, Huang is treated like a megastar, with fans crowding him for autographs and selfies as journalists follow him to the barber shop and his favourite night market.
“He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm,” noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute.

“A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses. But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan,” he said, calling Huang “unusually friendly.”
Over the years, Nvidia has taken care to project a drama-free image of Huang.

But the former employee painted a more nuanced picture, describing a “very paradoxical” individual fiercely protective of his employees but also capable, within Nvidia’s executive circle, of “ripping people to shreds” over major mistakes or poor choices. — AFP

a5dca6e4aaf379a8: SINGAPORE, Nov 9 — Three Singaporean tourists were injured in Taiwan after the taxi in which they were travelling was hit by a car from the opposite direction that crossed into their lane.

8bf5e14d887c6f7d: FRANKFURT: German exports rose more than expected in September on strong demand from other European countries, official data showed Monday, the latest positive sign for the manufacturing powerhouse.
Exports increased 2% from the previous month to €141.1 billion (US$158 billion), rebounding after two months of declines, statistics agency Destatis said.
That was above a rise of 0.5% forecast by analysts surveyed by the financial data firm FactSet.
It follows recent positive growth and manufacturing data, fuelling hopes that Europe's biggest economy has turned a corner after a long period of stagnation.
The September export data was lifted by a 3.5% increase in shipments to other EU countries, according to the provisional data from Destatis.
But exports to China fell over 5%, extending a downward trend as the country's manufacturers increasingly compete with German companies in sectors ranging from automobiles to chemicals.
Shipments to the US, the biggest destination for German goods, slipped by 0.5%. Germany's trade with the world's largest economy has been hit hard by US President Donald Trump's tariff blitz.
Imports rose 4.2% in September from the previous month to €125.5 billion, and Germany's trade surplus narrowed to €15.6 billion.

Despite higher energy prices triggered by the US war against Iran, the German economy is expected to grow in 2026 at its fastest pace in several years, lifted by higher government spending on defence and infrastructure.
be2309e4d221f2e2: ANTALYA (Turkiye), Nov 9 — The COP31 climate talks kicked off today with an early fight over money as the UN’s chief urged world leaders to “get serious” about tackling the crisis after a year of devastating weather extremes.
Antonio Guterres made his plea as thousands of participants descended on a sprawling expo centre in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya for the UN’s annual two-week climate conference.

The summit comes after a year of punishing heatwaves in Europe, major wildfires in Indonesia and catastrophic floods in Nepal, with an exceptionally strong El Nino weather phenomenon fuelling more climate chaos.
“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” Guterres said in a statement.

The UN secretary-general urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.
The COP31 opening ceremony opened an hour-and-a-half late without explanation.
Negotiators had been locked in discussions late Sunday over demands by developing nations to include items on climate finance in the official agenda.
“This has already been a difficult start for COP31,” said Jasper Inventor, head of Greenpeace’s COP31 delegation.

Under UN climate agreements, developed countries, which are historically responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions, have provided financial support to help developing nations adapt to climate impacts and transition to cleaner energy. But poorer countries say the sums remain insufficient.

Inventor said developed countries took a “hard line” over whether to include a platform, agreed at COP30 in Brazil last year, aimed at discussing how wealthy nations should provide funds to developing nations.
A source familiar with the talks said the “climate finance work programme” would be included in the agenda.

African countries had also pushed for the agenda to include the tripling of adaptation finance, which aims to help poorer nations pay for measures such as building sea walls or planting drought-resistant crops.
The source said there would be no separate agenda point on tripling of adaptation finance but that it would be discussed under other items.
A senior European Union official warned last week that there would be “no political will” for extra funding pledges at COP31.
Observers say few major breakthroughs are expected at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war with Iran and Russia’s conflict in Ukraine.

The long-term climate outlook is bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global temperatures were on course to exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement.
Fossil fuel fight
Turkiye is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference but raised concerns over how it would work.

The two sides have celebrated their cooperation so far, with COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, and Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen raising their clasped hands above their heads to applause during the opening ceremony.
The partners have branded the summit as the “implementation COP”, focusing on turning commitments into concrete action after years of pledges and ambitious announcements.
“We know that delay carries one of the heaviest costs in climate action,” Kurum said.
Turkiye is inviting countries to join a voluntary “electrification” pledge to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.
‘Clean’ electrification?
But the initiative could become a source of friction.
The European Union has called for “clean” electrification, a term that could spark debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.
Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.
COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.
Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary “roadmap” with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who will be among leaders addressing COP31 later this week, was due to arrive late Monday, fresh from a re-election win that activists hailed as a victory for climate change.
But climate diplomacy is still missing a major player as climate-sceptic US President Donald Trump has not sent officials to COP31.
A US congressional delegation, however, will come to Antalya, with Democrats beaming after last week’s historic US midterm election win. — AFP
b4935bb3fa9a20b4: KOTA KINABALU, Nov 9 — A Sabah Fire and Rescue Department search dog died a day after completing its final search-and-rescue mission, bringing nearly nine years of service with the department’s K9 unit to an end.
The 10-year-old Labrador Retriever, named Lexi, was found dead in its kennel at 6.15am last Friday, according to a report by Harian Metro.
Lexi had taken part in a search operation for a missing person in Kampung Pulutan Membawang, Menggatal, on November 5, making it the dog’s final assignment with the rescue team.
Sabah Fire and Rescue Department K9 unit chief Calvin Joe Jeafery said Lexi had been accompanied by its handler, fireman Arthur Anderson Walter, during the operation.
After returning to the station, Lexi was bathed and fed as part of its usual care routine, with Calvin saying the dog finished its food and showed no change in behaviour.
However, personnel found it unresponsive when they called its name during a routine kennel inspection the following morning, and further checks confirmed that it had died.
Calvin said Lexi had a medical history that included stage-two heart disease and a growth on its gums.
The dog had been under veterinary supervision and received treatment including antibiotics, gastric medication and anti-inflammatory drugs.
Its cause of death has yet to be established, pending a post-mortem report from the Sabah Veterinary Services Department, he said.
During its service, Lexi was trained in wilderness search-and-rescue operations, specialising in locating missing people in forests and other challenging terrain.
The dog joined the Sabah K9 unit after being acquired from the United Kingdom in 2017, and its final operation in Menggatal marked the close of a career spanning almost nine years.

093dee17953afbfa: BRUSSELS: The EU wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday, before ministers held their first discussions on a successor to Christine Lagarde.

Former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot and Spain's Pablo Hernandez de Cos, head of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), are the two candidates to replace Lagarde, who announced last month that she would step down in February.

0eb379a3880421ea: A Welsh music enthusiast has built an internet radio station that plays AI-generated tunes alongside human-made tracks without telling listeners which is which, to find out whether listeners really hate AI music or just the idea of it.

AI Slop FM is the creation of Mike Chaffin, who built and runs the station single-handedly from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire. By stripping away artist names, cover art, and any mention of AI, Chaffin hopes to find out what listeners really think when they have nothing but the music to go on.

The free 24/7 station asks listeners to rate tracks from S to E, tag how the music makes them feel, and leave written feedback. The most popular submissions will eventually make it into a weekly chart called the Slop 40, giving creators something that can be hard to come by in the age of streaming: an actual audience.

Anyone can submit a track, including human musicians, although Chaffin has already discovered that not all of them are particularly keen on the idea. He told The Register that he had floated the idea to an unsigned musician friend who had sold around 600 albums, but was met with a rather nervous response.
"Wh, wh, why would I want to do that?" the musician reportedly asked, according to Chaffin, who said he had never heard his friend stutter before.
"It seems that there is a deep rooted fear of AI music in the industry," Chaffin said.

The station is still in beta, with Chaffin waiting for enough submissions to fill its schedule across different genres before opening it fully. He's already been pleasantly surprised by the quality of the music submitted, although he still listens to every track to make sure nobody is trying to pass off Bohemian Rhapsody as their own work.
Among the early offerings are what Chaffin describes as a developing genre of slightly rude protest songs about HR departments, along with an operatic epic about a blocked toilet.
"Some of which are hilarious," he said of the HR songs. As for the toilet opera, it "runs through my head about once a day, whether I like it or not."

Chaffin believes the sheer volume of music uploaded to streaming platforms means plenty of perfectly decent tracks never find an audience, whether a person or a machine made them. He hopes AI Slop FM will give some of those overlooked creations a chance to be heard.
"You don't have to have published your creations to upload. Just to own the rights," he explained.
Tracks that don't make the Slop 40 could still get another outing, with plans for genre-specific stations offering unsuccessful submissions a second chance.
The bigger question is what happens when listeners start rating AI-generated music more highly than the human competition, but Chaffin isn't particularly worried about that.
"If the machines win then their creators clearly deserve to be heard, deserve an audience. If the musicians win, then that's reassuring for them."

He also wants to see how the station's eventual top five or top ten compares with the official music charts, although with submissions having only recently opened, there are no results to pore over just yet.
"Everyone has an opinion on music before a note has been heard, by the genre, the label, the name or the cover art," Chaffin said. "We strip all that away, tracks are judged purely on the music."

Whether listeners ultimately prefer human musicians or their algorithmically assisted rivals remains to be seen. Either way, somewhere in Carmarthenshire, an opera about a blocked toilet is proving rather difficult to flush from its listener's memory. ®
f8e8d17bf7036862: PARIS, Nov 9 — European top diplomats were today set to press US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to ensure any settlement in the war with Russia is fair to Ukraine and steer clear of any new escalation with Iran, at talks of the G7 group in Paris.

The meeting of ministers from the leading industrialised nations of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States will provide Europe and its allies with a chance to air preoccupations with their US counterpart.

Russia’s war against Ukraine following the February 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbour is grinding towards its fifth anniversary. And Washington is still not ruling out new attacks against Iran even after the defeat of President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the midterms.

The meeting coincides with US-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled for tomorrow and Wednesday on ending the Ukraine war, with Europe concerned Kyiv must not be forced to accept disadvantageous conditions and that the US could offer Russia new security guarantees over the heads of the Europeans.

“For Europe, it is clear: we do not need to establish a new security architecture for Europe,” said German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul as he headed to the talks, adding Europe “must have a place at the table”.
‘Cannot afford’
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said yesterday that Europeans will be represented at the Abu Dhabi talks, with France also participating.
Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a “very big” deal with Russia involving not only Ukraine but “all of Europe”.

But before leaving for Paris, Rubio said the post-war security infrastructure of Europe is “one of the key topics that’s been raised repeatedly in every conversation any time negotiations have been discussed.”
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he noted.
On Iran, Trump has not ruled out new strikes, including at so-called Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.
Europeans, however, are eager to see a resolution and shipping traffic return to normal in the Strait of Hormuz energy transit hub.
Trump allayed some fears by telling CNN it was “highly unlikely” that fighting would resume.
“We certainly cannot afford any military escalation at this point,” said Wadephul, adding the G7 talks would “focus on identifying ways to ensure it is indeed avoided”.
Rubio warned however there had been “no progress” in talks with Iran whose demands he said were “simply not just unacceptable but, in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”
‘Not uncommon’

The G7 ministerial meeting, one of the final acts of the French G7 presidency that saw President Emmanuel Macron host Trump for the leaders’ summit this summer in the lakeside resort of Evian, had long been scheduled to be held in the southern port city of Marseille.
But at the last minute the event was moved to Paris, with only scheduling reasons given for the change.
The visit by Rubio — seen by US media as a potential candidate to succeed Trump — is his first abroad since the midterms. Washington will in 2027 take over the G7 presidency from France.
“It is not uncommon to have a division of power in this country,” Rubio said, alluding to the fact that Trump will now see both houses of Congress controlled by the Democrats.

The sidelines of the meeting will also see the French finance ministry hosting on Monday a donor conference to raise funds to repair the dome protecting the nuclear reactor that exploded in Ukraine’s Chernobyl in 1986 after it was damaged in a Russian strike last year.

Around €500 million (RM2.2 billion) is required but only just over half has been raised so far, with a target date of spring 2027 to muster the rest of the funds, the French finance ministry told AFP.

Even though the meeting was moved to Paris, Marseille will still host the launch of a network of 14 global ports uniting to combat drug trafficking, which has become a major scourge in the southern city, Barrot said. — AFP

0cd99ca5b269d52d: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 9 — The National Cyber Security Agency (Nacsa) recorded 5,110 cybersecurity incidents from January to September this year, compared with 5,837 incidents last year.

Nacsa chief executive Dr Megat Zuhairy Megat Tajuddin said the higher number of incidents recorded last year was largely driven by intrusion attempts and potential attacks, which were detected at an early stage.

He said Nacsa’s National Cyber Coordination and Command Centre (NC4) had also issued nine alerts and advisories in October and November this year, concerning security vulnerabilities affecting National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities and government agencies.

“It is important to understand that not all cybersecurity incidents have the same impact, and Nacsa’s main focus is on incidents which have the potential to disrupt the country’s essential services,” he told Bernama here today.

He said the cybersecurity incidents recorded included a ransomware attack on Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd in March 2025, which caused disruptions at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) for more than 10 hours.

Commenting on the viral Live Map & Ranking display, which placed Malaysia among the countries receiving the highest number of cyber attacks, Megat Zuhairy said the figures were based on monitoring through specific cyber security products and platforms, widely used by organisations in Malaysia.
“The sensors installed enable proactive monitoring of detected cyber activities and traffic, providing an overview based on data from these sources.

“Additionally, Malaysia is one of the key data centre hubs globally, and this position means that a large volume of international internet traffic passes through the country, either as a target of cyber attacks, or as a transit route to other destinations,” he said.
Megat Zuhairy said the display did not reflect the overall cyber security situation of a country, as a comprehensive assessment would need to take into account various other factors and data sources.
These include actual cyber security incidents, as detected activities or attempted attacks do not necessarily mean that an organisation has experienced an incident or system breach.

He said there was currently no specific global ranking or report comparing countries, based on actual cyber attack incidents. However, based on the National Cyber Threat Level (NCTL) assessment, Malaysia’s cyber threat level remained moderate, while the country was placed in Tier 1 under the Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI).
He added that Malaysia was also preparing for the transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), to address developments in quantum computing technology.
Megat Zuhairy said individuals were also targets of cyber threats, particularly through the hacking of social media, email and online banking accounts.
He reminded the public to understand the difference between account hacking and online scams, so that appropriate action could be taken if they encountered such situations.

“Hacking occurs when another party gains unauthorised access to an account or system. Early warning signs include login notifications from unrecognised devices or locations, passwords being changed without the account owner’s knowledge, or messages being sent from one’s own account without authorisation.
“Scams, on the other hand, occur when victims are deceived into voluntarily handing over money or information, for example, through calls, messages or fake offers,” he said.

Megat Zuhairy also urged users whose accounts had been compromised to immediately change their passwords, activate multi-factor authentication (MFA) and report the matter to the relevant platform provider.
Victims of scams involving money transfers, meanwhile, should contact their banks and the National Scam Response Centre (NSRC) via its hotline at 997.
“Authentic precautionary measures are generally simple and practical, such as activating MFA, keeping devices updated and refraining from sharing personal information.
“The public should also be wary of posts which do not cite clear sources, use an urgent tone, or recommend drastic measures such as withdrawing all their savings,” he said. — Bernama

111b66d97ab01eca: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies.

In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed, the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.

Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles.

But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?

Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress.

The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year.

Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study.

The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes.

In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe, which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.

But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels. Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year.

The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms. CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data. It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company. Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours.

There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels. Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy.

Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned. AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services.

The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy. It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly.

Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality. But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms.

Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals. At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast.

Industry leaders must implement the technology in the ways that promise to do the most to drive down emissions. Corporate customers should select models with the lowest environmental impacts and opt to work with the AI developers doing the most to reduce their climate footprint. And states and regions need to do more to incentivize or require all these companies to operate in more responsible ways.
The need has never been more apparent.
Mary Nichols is distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board.
Jeremy Tamanini is the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm.
daed6fa86fdbaa3d: DUNGUN, Nov 9 — A total of 69 participants in the Projek Berkelompok Kelapa Kampung Dendang, here, claim that their income has been affected since the beginning of this year due to an influx of imported coconuts in the market from Indonesia since the start of the year.

Overall, the participants of the group project planted 5,000 coconut trees over an area of 20 hectares in 2009 and started yielding results in 2012.

Mohamed Zakaria said that currently, the coconuts produced by the project’s participants are being purchased by the Federal Agricultural Marketing Authority (Fama) at a price of RM1.10 each to help market the growers’ produce following the influx of imported coconuts in the market, compared to RM2.50 each which were sold to wholesalers and traders previously.

He said that the situation caused some of the participants’ coconut plantations to no longer be properly managed, even though the trees were still producing yields.
Unsold coconuts pile up following an influx of supply from Indonesia since early this year, affecting their income, during a site visit in Kampung Dendang, Dungun November 9, 2026. — Bernama pic
“If this situation continues, we are worried that more participants will decide to leave this project because the sales results can no longer provide returns like before,” he said.

"The customers have to trust the refurbished equipment and have to trust the process. And I think one of the things that we have to be better at as a whole is that we kind of need to have a standard methodology regarding verification."

Work on verification standards with vendors including HP, Lenovo, and Dell is ongoing, Molberg said. He also argued that lifecycle services should be built into purchasing decisions rather than added three or four years later.
