a40b144ab5da56eb: From a layperson’s perspective, following the legal back-and-forth in the Malaysian courts can be rather taxing.
It often appears to be a war of words, legal arguments, constitutional interpretations and courtroom strategies, all aimed at persuading the presiding judge or judges.

Beneath the pomp and pageantry inherited from the British legal system, however, lie issues of profound constitutional significance that may or may not affect our lives today, but could have far-reaching consequences for generations to come.

When Malaysia was formed in 1963, several safeguards were negotiated to protect the interests and autonomy of North Borneo (now Sabah). Among these was Point 11 of the Inter-Governmental Committee (IGC) Report, under the heading tariffs and finance.
It provided that “North Borneo should retain control over its own finances, development and tariffs, with the right to formulate its own taxation policies and raise loans on its own credit”.

One can argue that the spirit and substance of this safeguard are found in the constitutional expression of Article 112C of the Federal Constitution, read together with Section 2(1) of Part IV of the Tenth Schedule and Clauses (1), (3) and (4) of Article 112D.

These provisions form the constitutional basis for Sabah's entitlement to a special grant equivalent to two-fifths (40%) of the net revenue derived by the federal government from Sabah, subject to the relevant constitutional provisions.

Former Sabah minister Yap Pak Leong revived the historical significance of this arrangement, maintaining that the 40% revenue-sharing arrangement was a fundamental condition underpinning Sabah's decision to join in the formation of Malaysia.
"Right from the start, I emphasised this share of 2/5 revenue to be a condition for Sabah to become part of Malaysia.”
He further stressed that without this safeguard being enshrined in the Federal Constitution, Sabah would not have agreed to participate in the formation of Malaysia.

The role Sabah and Sarawak played in forming Malaysia must be recognised, unlike the federated states of Malaya. The Borneo states negotiated separate terms under the IGC, one of which is Sabah’s entitlement to 40% revenue sharing of all taxes collected in Sabah.

From what I understand, the federal government is not objecting to Sabah’s right to the 40% revenue sharing, but to the High Court judgment on Oct 17, 2025, in favour of the Sabah Law Society (SLS), directing the federal and state government to commence a review within a stipulated period.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim himself promised during the last state election that the government would not appeal the High Court’s decision, but for whatever reasons, it seems he has reneged on that promise to the Sabah people.
On another point, one cannot help but question the position taken by the state government in these proceedings.
Having entered the case as an intervener at a relatively late stage, the state government appears caught between competing legal and political considerations.
Yet, arguably, it should have been at the forefront pursuing Sabah's constitutional entitlement.
The state government possesses the political mandate, institutional authority and constitutional standing to negotiate directly with the federal government.

Rather than allowing the matter to become an extended courtroom battle initiated by SLS on behalf of the people of Sabah, it should be exercising that authority to secure a meaningful and just resolution for Sabah's 47 "lost years".

In another case, another NGO, Sabah Action Body Advocating Rights (Sabar) has taken the federal government to court on February 27, 2025, disputing the validity of the Territorial Sea Act (TSA) 2012, which limits the State's maritime boundary to just three nautical miles.

While the Sabah state government may have its own reasons for not initiating legal challenges regarding Sabah's rights, and Sabahans are not privy to their arguments, it is only fair to ask where the Sabah government stands in relation to these key court challenges.
The position is unlike in Sarawak, where the state government has led similar challenges.

Importantly, after more than six decades since Sabah agreed to become a part of Malaysia, one uncomfortable reality remains: according to official statistics, Sabah continues to record the highest poverty incidence in the country.
That is a sobering indictment of the development gap that persists despite Sabah's immense natural resources and its contributions to the Malaysian federation.
The legal arguments may continue. Appeals may be filed, constitutional provisions may be debated, and lawyers may argue over jurisdiction, procedures and remedies.
But beyond the courtroom, ordinary Sabahans continue to face the realities of poverty, inadequate infrastructure, water and electricity shortages, and limited economic opportunities.

The fundamental question is this: after more than 60 years in the Malaysian federation, should Sabahans still have to fight in court for constitutional assurances that were meant to protect their interests from the very beginning?

The 40% entitlement should not be treated as a political bargaining chip, nor should its fulfilment be reduced to a battle of legal technicalities. It is a constitutional matter rooted in the historical terms and safeguards surrounding the formation of Malaysia.
It is about justice, constitutional accountability and the future of Sabah.
The people of Sabah have waited long enough. Following Lord Hewart CJ’s well-known dictum, “justice must be seen to be done”.

c6b1da594a8a831d: Over 60% of Floridian voters voted to cut property taxes, which has been surging in recent years. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes. Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break known as a homestead exemption would go from the current US$51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New Florida residents who buy a home would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis. But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments. While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off. How Amendment 3 would work Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes. In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses. So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters. Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits. But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached. Who pays the bill? Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments. With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups. Essential public services, including fire and police departments, could face sharp budget cuts due to the shortfall from lower property taxes. Orange County Fire Rescue Department via AP This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages. State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees. Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event. In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties. And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll. A looming affordable housing crunch? Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing. When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall. From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs. Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift.
